true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the width/height variant

The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first, so the width/height variant is dead code. Any existing caller that invokes `downsize(from, to, width, height)` will now have its `height` argument bound to the `opts` parameter; when `optimize` evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer it raises `TypeError (no implicit conversion of Integer into Hash-like)`. Either remove the old signature entirely or rename/merge the two methods so the four-argument form still works.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB limit ignores admin-configured max upload sizes

validateUploadedFile now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, and the 413 handler at line 246 similarly hardcodes 10 MB instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. This silently disables the `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` site settings on the client: admins who set a lower limit will see users attempting uploads up to 10 MB (which then fail server-side with a confusing error for attachments), and admins who set a higher limit will get an incorrect 'file too large' rejection in the browser. This looks like leftover debug/test code (the PR description is 'Test 1') and should be reverted to read the settings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop can never bring very large images under the limit and ignores downsize failures

The retry loop runs at most 5 iterations, each downsizing to '80%', so the best possible reduction is to 0.8^5 ≈ 33% of the original size. An image more than ~3x `max_image_size_kb` will still exceed the limit when the loop exits, and the oversized file is then passed to `Upload.create_for`, which will reject it — the user waits through 5 ImageMagim/ImageOptim passes only to get the same failure the feature was supposed to prevent. Additionally, the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is never checked: if conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image or ImageMagick policy limits), the loop blindly retries five times and may hand a truncated/corrupted tempfile to `Upload.create_for`. The loop should either compute the exact target percentage needed in one pass or check the downsize result and bail out with a clear error.

Hardcoded 10MB download cap regresses API uploads for sites with larger configured limits

The API URL-download path changed `FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. On sites where an admin has raised `max_image_size_kb` above 10240 KB, remote images larger than 10 MB can no longer be fetched via the API at all (the download silently returns nil due to `rescue nil`, leading to a confusing failure downstream), even though such uploads were previously allowed. The cap should be derived from the setting (e.g. `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` plus some headroom to allow downsizing), not hardcoded.

allow_animation option never applies to uploads because animated-GIF detection relies on the file extension

The controller passes `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but `OptimizedImage.optimize` (optimized_image.rb line 155) only chooses the animated code path when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The `from` path here is an uploaded/action-dispatched tempfile (RackMultipart-* or discourse-upload-*), which never ends in `.gif`, so animated GIFs are always processed through `convert #{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame. Even on sites with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, every oversized animated GIF upload is silently stripped down to a single static frame — permanent loss of the original animation since the tempfile is downsized in place.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update and destroy raise NoMethodError (500) for unknown or malformed requests

`update` does `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then passes the result to `save_host`, which calls `host.host = ...` — if no record exists with that id, `host` is nil and the controller raises NoMethodError. `destroy` (line 15-16) has the same problem with `host.destroy`. Additionally, `save_host` dereferences `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` without checking that the `:embeddable_host` key exists, so a request without that payload also 500s. These should render a 404/validation error instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Category and embeddable_host fabricators are in swapped files

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now contains only the `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` definition, while all the category fabricators (:category, :diff_category, :happy_category, :private_category) were moved into `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The fabricators still register globally so tests pass, but the file organization is inverted and will confuse anyone maintaining these specs; each fabricator should live in its own named file.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Raw string interpolation of host values into INSERT SQL

The migration builds `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts ... VALUES ('#{h}', ...)` by interpolating each line of the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting directly into SQL. A host value containing a single quote (a typo like `o'brien.com`) will break the SQL statement and abort the migration mid-way, and in general this is an injection vector. The values should be quoted/escaped (e.g. via `sanitize_sql_array` or `quote`) or inserted through ActiveRecord models.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes with NoMethodError when embed_category setting was never customized

The migration runs `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. Discourse only writes a site_settings row when a value differs from its default, so on a fresh install (or any site where the admin never changed `embed_category`) this query returns zero rows and `[0]` is nil, making `[0]['id']` raise NoMethodError and the migration fail. The `if category_id == 0` fallback never gets a chance to run. The same nil-dereference pattern exists on line 15 for `uncategorized_category_id`. The migration must handle empty result sets before indexing into them.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
"is false if embeddable_host is blank" test no longer tests the blank-host case

After the refactor, this test no longer creates any embeddable host but also does not set `embed_truncate`, so the assertion `topic.expandable_first_post? == false` passes merely because `embed_truncate` is false by default — not because there is no embeddable host. The old test explicitly set `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts = nil`. Since `expandable_first_post?` no longer consults hosts at all (app/models/topic.rb line 869), the test name is misleading and the guard it claims to verify was removed; it should be renamed or updated to reflect the new condition.

Embed referer check now performs an uncached, unindexed DB query on every request

`EmbeddableHost.host_allowed?` / `record_for_host` run `where("lower(host) = ?", ...)` against the database, and `EmbedController#ensure_embeddable` calls this on every `/embed/comments` and `/embed/count` request — these are hit on every page view of every embedding site. The previous implementation read a cached in-memory site setting. The new `embeddable_hosts` table has no index on `host` (and none is added in the migration), so each embed request is a full table scan. Add an index and/or cache the host list.

New admin controllers have no behavioral tests

Both new controller specs (Admin::EmbeddableHostsController and Admin::EmbeddingController) only assert `Controller < Admin::AdminController`. There are no tests for create/update/destroy of embeddable hosts (including the nil-id 500 behavior), for the category_id defaulting to uncategorized, or for the embedding show/update endpoints. The migration's data conversion from the old site settings is also untested.

PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a silent no-op

The `update` action re-serializes `@embedding` without reading or persisting anything from the request body. The route (config/routes.rb line 139) exposes a PUT endpoint and the admin controller's `saveChanges` action calls `embedding.update({})`, but the server discards whatever is sent. Any client that believes it saved embedding settings gets a success response while nothing was stored. Either the action should apply and persist the submitted attributes, or the route/action and the client `saveChanges` code should be removed.

Validation permits a port but host matching never includes it, so such hosts can never work

The format regex accepts hosts like `localhost:3000` (the `(:[0-9]{1,5})?` group), and `before_validation` only strips the scheme and path — not the port. However `record_for_host` compares against `uri.host`, which excludes the port. So an admin can save an embeddable host containing a port, it validates fine, and then every embed request from that host is rejected because `localhost:3000 != localhost`. Either strip/forbid the port or compare on host:port.

create_table with force: true silently drops an existing embeddable_hosts table

`create_table :embeddable_hosts, force: true` will drop and recreate the table if it already exists (e.g. created by a plugin or a partially-applied migration) without warning, destroying any rows. `force: true` is a development convenience and should not ship in a production migration. Also, the raw `execute` statements inside `change` make the migration non-reversible despite using `change`.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TopicsController#unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser record

In the new `unsubscribe` action, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (any logged-in user can visit /t/<any topic>/unsubscribe for a topic they have never viewed, posted in, or been emailed about — the URL is trivially guessable since it is just the topic URL plus /unsubscribe). The code then calls `tu.notification_level` on nil, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500. The action should create/normalize the record via `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` like `set_notifications` does, which also correctly sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` and publishes the MessageBus `notification_level_change` event that the direct `tu.save!` path skips.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new TopicsController#unsubscribe behavior

The new `unsubscribe` action implements toggle semantics, slug-mismatch 301 redirects, permission handling, and TopicUser mutation, but no request/controller specs were added for any of it (the only test touched in the PR is the message_builder spec, which merely adds an `unsubscribe_url` option without asserting the topic link appears in the body or List-Unsubscribe header). Given the reachable nil crash and the CSRF-prone GET noted above, this endpoint needs specs covering: user with no TopicUser record, watching vs regular vs muted starting levels, wrong-slug redirect, and inaccessible topic.

State-changing GET endpoint is vulnerable to CSRF and accidental triggering The new `unsubscribe` action mutates the user's notification level on a GET request. A logged-in user's browser can be made to hit this URL cross-site (e.g. an `` on an attacker page sends session cookies), silently muting or un-muting topics for the victim. Additionally, because the handler *toggles* state (watching/tracking -> regular, otherwise -> muted), any repeated visit — a page refresh, browser pre-render/prefetch of the email link, or a scanner following links in an open session — flips the user's notification level again, potentially re-subscribing someone who just unsubscribed. State changes should be made via a POST endpoint (the email link can go to a page with a button, or use a per-user token), not on GET.

Unsubscribe toggle does not actually unsubscribe watching/tracking users, contradicting the email text

The controller demotes watching/tracking users only to `regular` on the first click. At the `regular` notification level the user still receives notifications when they are replied to, mentioned, or quoted, yet the email footer added in this PR says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" and the client page says "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>". A watching user who clicks the unsubscribe link in the email will keep getting reply/mention emails for that topic. If the intent is a toggle, the messaging is wrong; if the intent is unsubscribe, the level should go to `muted` (or the UI should make the choice explicit before mutating).

unsubscribe_link locale now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email builder caller that doesn't pass it

The `unsubscribe_link` translation was changed to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder` merges its opts into template_args, so any caller using `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationData` when building the body (`body << I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`) or the HTML part, and the email will fail to send. This is an undocumented new contract on the MessageBuilder API — nothing enforces or documents that `unsubscribe_url` must accompany `add_unsubscribe_link`, so plugins or future mailers that only pass `add_unsubscribe_link` will break. The builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. fall back to the preferences URL) or omit that sentence when it is absent, and this requirement needs a test.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs database writes during model validation

BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation chain. Validation must be side-effect free: UsersController#create calls user.valid? (line 168) and then user.save, so every signup attempt runs validation twice and match_count/last_match_at are incremented twice per attempt. Any other code path that calls valid? on a User (e.g. User#change_username calls valid?) also performs an unexpected UPDATE on the blocked_emails table during what should be a read-only check. The collected statistics are therefore inflated and unreliable, and writes occur at times no caller expects them. Move the counter update out of the query path (e.g. record the hit only when a signup is actually rejected, or use a separate logging step).

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

should_block? looks up BlockedEmail.where(email: email) with an exact string match. The rest of the codebase normalizes emails (Email.downcase is used in UsersController#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email), but nothing downcases the value here, and User#email is stored as submitted. A blocked address like 'spammer@example.com' can be re-used by signing up with 'Spammer@Example.com' or 'SPAMMER@example.com', defeating the entire blocklist feature. The lookup (and ideally the stored value) should compare downcased emails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Any server email error permanently marks the email invalid with a misleading message

After a failed createAccount, the controller adds the email to rejectedEmails whenever the server response contains errors.email. This includes errors that are not about validity, such as 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist/blacklist 'not allowed from that email provider' message. Once added, emailValidation shows the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') reason for that address with no way to distinguish causes, so a returning user who already has an account is told their email is simply invalid. Only add to rejectedEmails when the error is actually a blocked/invalid-email error (e.g. have the server send a distinguishable error code), or surface the server's real error message in the validation reason.

No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator

The EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch, and it stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely. The domain whitelist/blacklist logic (email_in_restriction_setting? and both setting branches) was moved verbatim from User#email_validator into this new class but has no direct tests here, and no integration test covers that creating a User with an email present in blocked_emails actually fails. There is also no test for the case-sensitivity behavior of the blocked lookup. The core behavior of this PR (blocked emails reject signups end-to-end) is untested.

Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates under concurrency

should_block? does a read-modify-write: it loads the record, does record.match_count += 1 in Ruby, then record.save. Two concurrent requests for the same blocked email both read the same count and both write count+1, so one increment is silently lost. Since this counter is the mechanism for tracking how often a blocked email attempts to register, it will undercount. Use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now]).

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of exact origin comparison

The resize handler accepts messages when `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is false, i.e. when the message origin appears anywhere as a substring of discourseUrl. That is not an equality check: any origin that happens to occur inside the discourseUrl string (e.g. as part of a path, or a shorter scheme/host prefix in some configurations) is accepted, and e.data.height is used unvalidated. The consequence is limited to resizing the iframe, but the check should compare `e.origin` against the exact expected origin (e.g. the parsed origin of discourseUrl) and the height coerced to a positive integer.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated into a JS string literal without escape_javascript

The layout does `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The referer is only validated to have a host equal to embeddable_host; its path/query can contain arbitrary characters (an attacker can send a request with a crafted Referer header directly — no control of a page on the host is needed). The value is placed in a single-quoted JavaScript string with no `j`/escape_javascript; it currently survives only because Rails' HTML escaping converts quotes to `'`, which then appears literally inside the script block, producing an invalid targetOrigin that makes postMessage throw a SyntaxError and breaks iframe resizing for such referers. It should be escaped with escape_javascript (and ideally the exact origin, not the full referer, used as targetOrigin).

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Stored XSS: embed URL interpolated unescaped into raw HTML footer TopicEmbed.import builds the "Imported from" footer with `"#{url}"` — the URL is interpolated into HTML with no escaping, and the resulting post is stored with cook_method raw_html (cooked = raw, bypassing the sanitizing Markdown pipeline) and rendered in app/views/embed/best.html.erb with `raw post.cooked`. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?:///`, which permits quotes, `>`, and attribute-breaking characters. An attacker can hit /embed/best with a crafted embed_url whose host matches embeddable_host (e.g. `http:///?'>

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view can never render

The ERb at line 6 reads `<%- end if %>` with no condition following the `if` modifier. When ERb compiles the template the generated Ruby ends with `end if`, which is a syntax error (unexpected end-of-input). Any request to /embed/best for which a TopicEmbed exists (the main success path of this feature) will raise ActionView::Template::Error instead of rendering the comments. The controller specs never render views (TopicView is mocked, no render_views), so CI does not catch this — a view-rendering test is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil or failing feed item aborts the entire feed import with no per-item error handling

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every RSS/Atom item has content; for plain RSS 2.0 feeds without content:encoded, simple-rss returns nil for `i.content`, so this line raises NoMethodError on the first such item and the whole poll is aborted. Similarly, any exception raised while importing one item (bad URL, PostCreator failure — note that if the post fails to save, TopicEmbed.import still calls TopicEmbed.create! with a nil topic_id, raising RecordInvalid inside the transaction) prevents all subsequent items from being imported. Each item should be processed with its own error handling (and nil content handled, e.g. falling back to i.description).

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated into a JS string literal without escape_javascript

The layout does `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The referer is only validated to have a host equal to embeddable_host; its path/query can contain arbitrary characters (an attacker can send a request with a crafted Referer header directly — no control of a page on the host is needed). The value is placed in a single-quoted JavaScript string with no `j`/escape_javascript; it currently survives only because Rails' HTML escaping converts quotes to `'`, which then appears literally inside the script block, producing an invalid targetOrigin that makes postMessage throw a SyntaxError and breaks iframe resizing for such referers. It should be escaped with escape_javascript (and ideally the exact origin, not the full referer, used as targetOrigin).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed and page fetches use open() with no timeout; a slow source hangs the job and the hourly schedule

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (and `open(url)` in TopicEmbed.import_remote) use Kernel#open with no read/open timeout. The scheduled job has `retry: false` and is also invoked synchronously from TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve on a user-triggered retrieve, so a hanging or very slow feed server blocks a Sidekiq worker indefinitely and stalls subsequent scheduled runs. open-uri should be given `open_timeout`/`read_timeout` (or a job-level timeout).

Only Gemfile_rails4.lock was updated; the default (Rails 3) lockfile is missing the new gems

The PR adds ruby-readability and simple-rss to the Gemfile and updates Gemfile_rails4.lock, but the repository's dual-boot setup (see the Bundler monkey patch at the top of the Gemfile) uses the default Gemfile.lock when booting in Rails 3 mode (`RAILS3` set), which per the diff was not regenerated. Any Rails 3-mode CI run or deployment will fail to resolve the new dependencies (TopicEmbed/poll_feed require them at runtime), so the Rails 3 lockfile needs the corresponding entries.

RSS item content imported as raw_html with no sanitization — stored XSS from feed content

poll_feed passes `i.content` (the raw HTML from the feed's content:encoded/body) straight into TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Post#cook then returns the raw string untouched, skipping the normal cooking/sanitizing pipeline, and best.html.erb renders it with `raw post.cooked`. Anyone who can influence the feed's HTML (compromised or malicious feed source at the admin-configured feed_polling_url) gets arbitrary JavaScript executed on the Discourse origin for every viewer, including logged-in staff. The readability path at least whitelists tags/attributes; the feed path has no equivalent. The imported HTML should be run through a sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

`force: true` added to an existing migration will drop an already-created top_topics table

This PR changes the previously shipped CreateTopTopics migration to `create_table :top_topics, force: true`. With force: true, create_table drops the table if it already exists; any environment that already ran the original migration and then re-runs it (db:migrate:redo, rebuilding from migrations rather than schema.rb) will silently lose all top_topics data. If the change was needed for test databases, it should be made in a separate migration or the test schema rebuilt, not by editing a released migration.

absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs that pass the http(s) regex

TopicEmbed.import only gates on `url =~ /^https?:///`, but absolutize_urls then calls `URI(url)` which raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs containing spaces or other invalid characters (e.g. `http://exa mple.com/post` or an unencoded `%zz`). Unlike TopicRetriever#invalid_host?, there is no rescue here, so a single malformed feed link (or a crafted embed_url) raises an unhandled exception. In PollFeed this aborts the remaining feed items; in RetrieveTopic the job fails. The URI parse should be guarded or the URL rejected up front with a full URI parse.

embed_url column is varchar(255); real URLs (plus the appended footer) can exceed it

The embed_url column is a Rails `string`, i.e. varchar(255) on PostgreSQL, with a NOT NULL constraint. Web page URLs frequently exceed 255 characters, and TopicEmbed.import additionally embeds the URL twice (href and text) into the post body; an over-long feed link will make the INSERT fail with 'value too long for type character varying(255)', aborting the import. The column should be text (or a larger limit) to match how URLs are stored elsewhere.

setnx/expire are not atomic; a crash between them permanently disables retrieval for a URL

retrieved_recently? performs `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies between the two calls (or the expire fails), the key exists with no TTL and the URL is considered 'recently retrieved' forever — the embed will never be fetched again through the throttled path, leaving the loading page reloading every 30 seconds indefinitely. A single SET key 1 EX 60 NX (or a Lua script) should be used instead.

The UI then shows an empty member list with currentPage=2 and totalPages=1 (so showingLast is false and 'next' keeps firing no-op requests at the same offset). false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Fallback locales are not loaded outside the controller request path, so fallbacks fail in jobs and mailers

With fallbacks enabled, when a key is missing in the current locale the I18n backend walks the fallback chain (user locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en). However I18n.translate in the accelerator only calls load_locale(config.locale), so the fallback locales' translation files stay unloaded unless someone explicitly called I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. That call is only made in ApplicationController#set_locale. Background jobs (Sidekiq), ActionMailer deliveries, rake tasks and console code set I18n.locale directly without ensure_loaded!, so a lookup for a key missing in e.g. :fr will probe :en (or the default locale) while its YAML files are not loaded and will return 'translation missing: fr.xxx' even though the English translation exists. The web UI shows the English fallback while emails/jobs show missing-translation strings. translate should also ensure the fallback locales (I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]) are loaded when fallbacks are configured.

FallbackLocaleList silently discards the standard I18n fallbacks assignment API

FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but overrides [] to always compute the chain from SiteSetting.default_locale, never consulting stored entries. The documented i18n extension point I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [:xx, :en] (used by plugins and by I18n::Locale::Fallbacks' own defaults mechanism, e.g. mapping language-specific fallbacks like pt to pt-BR) becomes a silent no-op: the assignment succeeds but is never read back. Any plugin relying on that API will appear to work while its fallbacks are ignored. Either delegate to super for explicitly-set locales or document that per-locale fallback registration is unsupported.

Fallbacks are now enabled in development/test, masking missing-translation regressions, and the PR ships no tests

Previously config.i18n.fallbacks = true was production/profile/cloud66-only; the new initializer enables fallbacks in every environment, including test. As a result, translations missing from a non-English locale now silently render English in the test suite, so tests can no longer detect keys that were not translated or were accidentally removed. On top of that, the PR adds no specs at all for the new behavior: nothing covers FallbackLocaleList ordering (user locale -> default -> en), ensure_loaded!, or that a key missing in the current locale resolves via the fallback chain. Add tests that assert the fallback resolution, and consider asserting on translation-missing detection separately so fallbacks don't hide gaps.

Translation cache key ignores SiteSetting.default_locale, so cached fallback results go stale when the default locale changes

The LRU cache key is "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}". With the new fallback chain, the cached result for a key missing in the user's locale also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (which is consulted by FallbackLocaleList#[] on every lookup). If an admin changes default_locale at runtime, translations previously resolved through the old default locale remain cached in the process-local LRU cache (size 300, so hot keys persist indefinitely) and users keep seeing the old language until eviction or restart. Nothing invalidates @cache when default_locale changes. The default locale (or a fallback-chain fingerprint) needs to be part of the cache key, or the cache must be flushed when the setting changes.

Basic coverage would have caught the crash-on-use defects (unsupported paginate kwarg, negative-offset slicing AssertionError, datetime key TypeError) and would guard the BasePaginator slicing change against regressions for existing consumers.

`enable_advanced_features` is not an accepted argument of `Endpoint.paginate`

The optimized branch calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. Sentry's `Endpoint.paginate` (in sentry/api/base.py) has no `enable_advanced_features` parameter — extra paginator constructor arguments must be passed via the `paginator_kwargs` dict. Any request with `optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser or global-access member will raise `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'` and return a 500, so the entire new code path can never succeed.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset "advanced" slicing raises AssertionError on Django QuerySets; the feature is non-functional

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indices are not allowed` when the queryset is not already evaluated, because there is no SQL equivalent of a negative OFFSET. The comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is simply false. Any client that sends a crafted cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses user-supplied strings like `0:-5:0` without validation) to an endpoint using this paginator gets a 500 instead of results. The whole 'advanced features' branch either crashes (negative offset) or is a byte-for-byte copy of BasePaginator.get_result with no behavioral difference (normal offsets), so it provides no optimization at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BasePaginator now silently clamps negative non-prev offsets to 0 instead of erroring

The base-class change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` alters behavior for any client that sends a cursor with a negative offset: previously `queryset[offset:stop]` would raise Django's negative-index AssertionError (a clear failure), while now a non-prev cursor with offset < 0 silently returns the first page of results again. A paging client that somehow ends up with a negative offset (or a maliciously crafted cursor) will re-receive page one and can loop over the same data indefinitely instead of surfacing an error. The is_prev branch is left unclamped, so the two paths are inconsistent: prev cursors with negative offsets still crash while next cursors silently reset. If negative offsets are meant to be invalid, both branches should reject them the way OffsetPaginator does with BadPaginationError.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes when used with a datetime sort key, which is how the audit logs endpoint uses it

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key copies Paginator's numeric implementation: `value = getattr(item, self.key); return int(math.floor(value) ...)`. The endpoint that instantiates it (organization_auditlogs.py) passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` object and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime`. build_cursor/_build_next_values call get_item_key on the first result of every page that has results, so every request to the audit logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` (by a superuser or org member with global access) will fail with a 500. DateTimePaginator exists precisely because datetimes need the strftime conversion; OptimizedCursorPaginator omits it. Its value_from_cursor has the matching defect (returns the raw cursor value instead of converting millis back to a datetime like DateTimePaginator does), so the cursor comparison in build_queryset would also be broken.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment claims negative offsets 'enable efficient reverse pagination' but they break the offset arithmetic in this module

The new comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets enable "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". That is not how the module works: _build_next_values and _build_prev_values compute offsets by adding/subtracting the page limit from the current offset, and consumers of these cursors slice querysets where negative offsets are unsupported (raising errors) or silently misbehave. The comment documents a capability that does not exist anywhere in the codebase and will mislead future maintainers into relying on it.

Direct `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` access will crash the consumer on messages that lack the field

process_batch now reads `end_timestamp_precise` with direct dict indexing. The existing consumer test message did not contain this field until this PR added it, which is evidence that messages without the field are representable in the topic (older producers or schema versions, plus any backlog present at deploy time). A KeyError raised inside process_batch propagates out of the RunTask/multiprocessing strategy and kills the consumer, stalling the whole partition — a much worse failure mode than defaulting the score (e.g. `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or 0` or falling back to the message timestamp). If the field is guaranteed by the current schema, that guarantee should at least be stated; the current code makes any pre-upgrade buffered message fatal.

New `optimized_pagination` query-parameter code path is undocumented and completely untested

This PR adds a new, undocumented request parameter (`optimized_pagination=true`) that switches a public (albeit EXPERIMENTAL) endpoint to a different paginator and enables an 'advanced features' mode, gated on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. There are no tests for this path anywhere in the PR, no API documentation for the new parameter, and no explanation of what it actually optimizes (the paginator is functionally identical to the default except for a negative-offset branch that crashes — see other findings). The PR description is just 'Test 2', which suggests this change was not reviewed as a deliberate feature. Given the path is broken for its only configured sort key (datetime), the lack of tests is why that was not caught.

New span eviction (zpopmin at 1000) silently drops span data with no metric or log, and can evict the segment's root span

The script now evicts the lowest-scored (oldest end_timestamp) members whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Unlike the previous behavior — where oversized segments were skipped at flush time with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log — this eviction is completely silent: there is no metric, no log, and no marker on the flushed segment, so the ongoing data loss is invisible to operators. Additionally, if the segment/root span is among the evicted members (possible whenever its end_timestamp is not the maximum, e.g. async traces), the segment is flushed without any root span, so no span gets `is_segment=True`, while the `span-buf:hrs:` key still reads "1" and forces the shorter root timeout. The limit is also hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, diverging from the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config (default 1001), which this PR leaves as a dead, unused parameter in SpansBuffer.__init__ (buffer.py line 150) — so the two limits can drift and the config can no longer be tuned from Python at all.

Redirect-following loop reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations with no justification, silently breaking deep segment trees

The loop bound was reduced tenfold and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:{...}` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with a stale `set_span_id`, and line 40 then writes an incorrect redirect mapping for the incoming span — the span is attached to the wrong segment and the trace is silently assembled incorrectly. There is no error signal when the cap is hit (redirect_depth is returned but nothing distinguishes 'resolved' from 'gave up'). Reducing the guarantee 10x needs at least a metric/alert on `redirect_depth == 1000` or a comment explaining why 1000 is safe; neither is present, and the diff gives no reason for the change.

zunionstore merges use the default AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting scores of payloads present in both keys

Both merge operations (`redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` at lines 47 and 53) omit an AGGREGATE argument, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same span payload exists in both source keys — which happens under Kafka's at-least-once delivery, e.g. a span delivered in one batch lands in the set keyed by its parent while a duplicate delivery in a later batch lands in the merged set — the resulting member's score is the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values. Since the score is the span's end timestamp used to order the zset, this silently doubles the timestamp. The consequences are that zpopmin eviction (which pops the lowest scores) evicts the wrong spans, and the flush-time iteration order no longer reflects chronological order. The previous sunionstore-based code had no score semantics so this was not an issue; the fix is to pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is computed from the closure `dataset` and request query, not the dataset/query actually being executed

Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, ...)`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset`, and the helper inspects `request.GET['query']` instead of the `query` argument. In the dashboard-widget split flow (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with different datasets (e.g. `discover`) and modified queries (e.g. `({query}) AND !event.type:transaction`). The upsampling decision can therefore be made against the wrong dataset/query than the one actually executed, yielding inconsistent counts between the split and non-split paths for the same widget.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental 'sentry-repo' git submodule added to the repository

The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing 'Subproject commit a5d2909...' plus (implicitly) a .gitmodules entry, creating a submodule that points back at the base commit of this same repository. This looks like a local debugging artifact committed by mistake. It will clone an extra copy of the repo for every developer/CI checkout and pollutes the repository layout; it should be removed before merge.

Substring match treats negated 'event.type:error' queries as error-focused, applying upsampling to non-error results

_is_error_focused_query checks `if "event.type:error" in query` on the raw query string. The Sentry search syntax negation `!event.type:error` contains that substring, so a query explicitly EXCLUDING errors (matching transactions/default events) is classified as error-focused. For the discover dataset, count() is then replaced with sum(sample_weight), producing wrong counts for a query that returns transactions (where sample_weight either doesn't exist or has different semantics). The check needs to parse the query (e.g. via the event_search parser) rather than doing substring matching.

The main entry point is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects, including its cache logic, is never tested

The unit tests cover only the private helpers (_are_all_projects_error_upsampled with mocked options, transform_query_columns..., _is_error_focused_query, _should_apply_sample_weight_transform). The public function that the endpoint actually calls — which composes the allowlist check, the 60s cache get/set, and the dataset check, and whose cache-hit branch (`cached_result and _should_apply_sample_weight_transform(...)`) is distinct logic — has no coverage. The SnubaParams built in setUp is never used. Cache-related regressions (e.g. caching the composite result instead of eligibility, or the invalidation helper) would not be caught.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling swallows all exceptions with bare 'except Exception: pass'

The new factory helper wraps both the context lookup and the float conversion in blanket `except Exception: pass`. If `contexts` has an unexpected shape (e.g. a list) or `client_sample_rate` is malformed, the failure is silently hidden, and the event is stored without a sample_rate — leading to tests that quietly exercise the non-upsampling path instead of failing loudly. The guard should be narrow (e.g. isinstance checks) rather than a bare except, and should at minimum surface unexpected error types.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code — allowlist changes are never propagated to the cache

The PR introduces a 60-second cache of the allowlist eligibility decision and provides `invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` with a docstring saying it 'should be called when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in the codebase calls it (no signal receiver on option changes, no hook where the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option is updated). Removing a project from the allowlist will leave stale `True` entries for up to 60s, during which queries against it use sum(sample_weight). If prompt invalidation is intended, the wiring is missing; if not, the function is dead code and should be removed.

upsampled_count declares result type 'number' while replacing count() whose result type is 'integer'

The new SnQLFunction 'upsampled_count' wraps its aggregate in toInt64 but sets `default_result_type="number"`, whereas the count() function it transparently replaces (via the alias `upsampled_count() as count`) is declared `integer`. Downstream consumers that key off the function's result type (zerofill, meta/serialization, response typing) may treat the aliased 'count' field differently than a normal count() query on the same endpoint, changing the API response shape for the same yAxis input. The result type should be 'integer' to match count().

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details zips error_ids against nodestore dict values, misaligning ids with data

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids`, calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)`, and then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node id, and missing nodes are simply absent from the result, so `events.values()` is not guaranteed to be in the same order as `error_ids` and is shorter whenever any lookup misses. When one error event is missing (e.g. expired from nodestore), every subsequent pairing shifts, so an `ErrorEvent` gets the wrong `id`, `title`, `message`, and `timestamp`. Downstream, `gen_request_data` uses these timestamps to interleave error messages chronologically with replay breadcrumbs, so the Seer summary will report the wrong errors at the wrong times. The correct approach is to look up each id individually from the returned mapping (e.g. `data = events.get(node_id)`), not to zip two independently ordered sequences.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hardcoded empty data

In `tableResultComponent`, when the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is on, the new branch renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` instead of the real result. All of the actual widget data is discarded: `result.data`, `result.meta`, `eventView`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, loading state, title, custom field renderers, and min column width are simply not passed. Any organization (or dogfooding/staff account) with that flag enabled will see completely empty dashboard/insights table widgets. The flag branch must either be wired to the real table data or not ship until it is; as written it silently breaks every table widget the moment the flag is flipped.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before the feature gate and request validation

The `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` call was placed at the very top of `post`, before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before schema validation. As a result the event fires for every request, including ones that are rejected with 404 (feature disabled) and 400 (invalid payload), so the metric counts denied and malformed requests as assemble attempts and cannot be used to measure actual usage of the endpoint. Additionally, for org-auth-token requests `request.user` may not be a real user, so `user_id` can be `None` for a large share of recorded events. Record the event after the feature check (and ideally after the body validates) so the analytics reflect real assemble attempts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

false_positives.candidate:
HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES are only filtered when a search query is active

The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` filter for `is_segment`, `project_id`, and `received` is applied only inside the branch that runs when `searchQuery.trim()` is non-empty; the early `return sorted;` for an empty search bypasses it. That means these internal noise attributes are shown in the span attributes panel in the normal (no-search) case and only disappear once the user types a search — the opposite of what a constant named HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES implies. The filter should be applied to `sorted` before the empty-search early return.

UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps doc comment says only LOGS is supported, but SPANS is now used

The doc comment on `UseTraceItemAttributeBaseProps.traceItemType` (moved into `explore/types.tsx` in this PR) states "The trace item type supported by the endpoint, currently only supports LOGS." However this same PR wires the hook family up for spans: `TransactionNameSearchBar` and `TraceItemSearchQueryBuilder` now pass `traceItemType: TraceItemDataset.SPANS` to `useGetTraceItemAttributeValues`/`useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys`. The comment is now wrong and will mislead future callers into avoiding the spans path.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use enforcement is not atomic (read-modify-write race)

In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup-code check does a read of the decrypted backupCodes array, an indexOf lookup, and then a separate prisma.user.update that writes back the whole array. Two concurrent sign-in requests using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so one single-use code authenticates twice; likewise two concurrent logins with different codes will each write their own copy of the array and the last write wins, resurrecting a code the other request already consumed. The code is also consumed (nulled and persisted) before next-auth finishes creating the session, so any later failure (JWT encode error, network drop mid-request) burns the code without a successful login. Single-use consumption should be made atomic/transactional and only committed once authentication has succeeded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Existing 2FA users can never obtain backup codes, and the error message tells them to do the impossible

Backup codes are only generated in the setup endpoint, which returns 400 TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled for any user who already has 2FA enabled. Users who enabled 2FA before this deploy have backupCodes = null, so the "Lost access" login path and the backup-code disable path always fail for them with MissingBackupCodes. The accompanying message ("No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." in common.json) is misleading because there is no settings flow that generates codes while 2FA is enabled — the only path is to disable 2FA (using the TOTP they may have lost) and re-enable it. Either a regeneration endpoint is needed or the message must tell the user their actual recovery option.

No tests for the core new functionality: logging in and disabling 2FA with a backup code

The e2e changes only exercise the backup-codes display step (download filename, copy toast, close button). None of the actually risky new code paths are tested: signing in with a backup code, a backup code being consumed (single-use), the incorrect-backup-code error path, the missing-backup-codes error path, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. The file itself contains a TODO acknowledging this, and the PR checklist states no tests were added for the feature. These server-side flows (including the code-consumption logic in next-auth-options.ts) can regress silently.

onEnable is only invoked via the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog any other way leaves the 2FA switch out of sync

After a successful enable, the modal moves to the DisplayBackupCodes step and onEnable() (which updates the settings page state, e.g. the two-factor switch) is only called from the "Close" button's onClick. If the user closes the dialog via ESC, the dialog's built-in close affordance, or onOpenChange (all wired directly to the onOpenChange prop), neither onEnable nor onCancel fires and the modal state is not reset. The security settings page will continue to show 2FA as disabled even though it is actually enabled in the database, and the dialog's internal step state persists for the next open. Previously onEnable was called directly on the successful enable response, so this is a regression introduced by deferring it to a user click.

tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes keyboard access

The show/hide password toggle button in PasswordField now has tabIndex={-1}, making it unreachable by keyboard in every password field across the app (login, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard-only users can no longer verify what they typed into a password field. If the goal was to stop Enter on the toggle from submitting the surrounding form, the button already has type="button"; excluding it from tab order is an accessibility regression rather than a fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Crash when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet

`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` followed by `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"` accesses `.integration` without optional chaining. When `destinationCalendar` is an empty array (which all the new fallback code paths in this PR now produce, e.g. `selectedDestinationCalendar ? [selectedDestinationCalendar] : []` in confirm.handler, handleCancelBooking, webhooks, etc.), destructuring yields `undefined` and `undefined.integration` throws a TypeError, breaking booking creation for Google-Meet-located events for users without a destination calendar. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration` which was null-safe. It must be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent/deleteEvent destination-calendar fallback is dead code and resolves to undefined

In `updateEvent` (and identically in `deleteEvent` at line 315) the new fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. This expression is only evaluated when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the `find` predicate compares each calendar's externalId against a falsy value and never matches. The result is always `undefined`, whereas the old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar.externalId`. Consequence: when a booking reference has no `externalCalendarId` (e.g. bookings whose destination calendar has no externalId, or older references), Google updates are sent with `calendarId: undefined` and deletes fall through to `"primary"`, meaning updates fail and deletes can target the wrong calendar. The fallback should look up the destination calendar matching the current credential (e.g. by `credentialId`) instead of comparing against the falsy `externalCalendarId`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Slug condition inverted: orgs now get a slug exactly when team billing is enabled

The change `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` → `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` inverts the original behavior while the adjacent `requestedSlug` line keeps the same condition as before. Previously the org Team record stored `slug` when billing was disabled and `requestedSlug` when billing was enabled; now `slug` is set when billing is enabled and nothing is set when it is disabled. This is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose and will break organization subdomain creation on instances where `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is false (no slug persisted) and double-set slug/requestedSlug when it is true.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
CalDAV BaseCalendarService ignores per-credential destination calendars, breaking multi-host collective events

`createEvent` filters the calendar list using only the first destination calendar's externalId (`mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId`). The `Calendar` interface was changed in this PR to pass `credentialId` to `createEvent` specifically so services can pick the destination matching the credential being used (as the Google service now does), but the CalDAV base class was not updated: its `createEvent(event)` signature doesn't accept `credentialId`, and when `EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents` invokes it once per host destination, every invocation still targets the first host's calendar. For a collective event with two CalDAV hosts, the second host's credentials are used to write into the first host's calendar URL (failing or creating the event in the wrong place) and the second host's calendar never receives the event. The same single-first-destination pattern also remains in the office365 and lark services, so multi-destination support effectively only works for Google Calendar.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancel-all-recurring branch deletes only the first calendar reference per booking using the organizer's credentials

In the `recurringEvent && allRemainingBookings` path, deletion iterates `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` (the organizer's credentials only) and, for each updated booking, deletes only `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` — the first calendar reference. With the new multi-reference support this PR introduces for collective events, co-hosts' calendar events are never deleted when cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, and the outer loop over `bookingCalendarReference` re-runs the same deletion for every reference, duplicating work. Deletion should use each reference's own `credentialId` and iterate all `_calendar` references per updated booking.

No automated tests cover the new multi-destination-calendar behavior, and payload expectations are inconsistent

The PR checklist states no tests were added, yet it changes a core type (`CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar`) consumed by every booking flow. The only test change is updating one expected webhook payload from `destinationCalendar: null` to `[]` (BOOKING_REJECTED) while BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED still expect `null` — reflecting inconsistent fallbacks (`handleNewBooking` uses `null`, `confirm.handler` uses `[]`). There is no test exercising a collective event with multiple hosts each having a calendar app (create/reschedule/cancel across two destination calendars), which is exactly the scenario the PR claims to fix; regressions like the Google update/delete fallback bug and the empty-array crash in EventManager.create would not be caught.

Reschedule merge deletes only the first calendar reference, leaving stale events on other hosts' calendars

`updateAllCalendarEvents` was extended to loop over all `_calendar` references (to support multiple destination calendars for collective events), but the merge branch that deletes the old booking's calendar events still uses `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))`, deleting only the first calendar reference. For a collective booking with events on two hosts' calendars, rescheduling to a new booking leaves the old event on the second host's calendar. The deletion should iterate all old `_calendar` references (using each reference's `credentialId`/`externalCalendarId`).

Team members' destination calendars are silently dropped when the organizer has none

So for a collective event whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose co-hosts do, all team destination calendars are discarded and no calendar events are created on any host's calendar (EventManager falls back to the organizer's first connected credential). The fallback should be `[]` (matching every other call site in this PR) or the team calendars should be assigned as the initial value.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dummy `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` overwrites real refresh tokens, including when sync is disabled

When the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token`, the code unconditionally sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This is not limited to the sync-enabled path — it also runs for the normal per-app schema. Microsoft's refresh-token endpoint legitimately omits `refresh_token` on refresh responses (the existing refresh token stays valid); previously Office365CalendarService preserved the old token via `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, but now the placeholder string "refresh_token" is spread over the real token and written to the DB. The next refresh will send `refresh_token=refresh_token` and fail with invalid_grant, breaking Office 365 calendar sync for existing non-sync users as a regression from this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys are broken and the schema strips all expiry/refresh fields

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no custom toString), so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown-optional }`. The comment claims "any property with a number is the expiry" but nothing like that is implemented — no expiry field is validated. Worse, zod's `z.object().parse` strips unknown keys by default, so when credential sync is enabled the returned `data` contains only `access_token` (plus the dummy refresh_token injected at line 26). Callers that persist this data — Google CalendarService (`data: { key }`) and Salesforce (`data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, ... } }`) — will save credentials that have lost `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, `instance_url`, `scope`, etc., permanently corrupting the stored credential. For Zoom, `newTokens.expires_in` is then undefined so `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` stores NaN.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response but callers expect library-specific objects (axios responses, hubspot tokens, gaxios res)

When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object. Several callers cannot handle that: HubspotCalendarService (CalendarService.ts:177-202) treats the return as a `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` (→ NaN expiryDate stored, `setAccessToken(undefined)`); zoho-bigin (CalendarService.ts:96) and zohocrm (CalendarService.ts:217) read `.data` on it (→ TypeError "Cannot set properties of undefined", crash); GoogleCalendarService (CalendarService.ts:94) reads `res?.data` from what used to be a gaxios response (`fetchTokens.res`), which is undefined on a fetch Response → `token.access_token` throws. Enabling the advertised sync feature breaks these apps outright; each caller needs the sync response normalized into the shape it expects.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
