false_positives.candidate:
Per-process SpansBuffer memory info double-counts Redis clusters, skewing the hard-backpressure ratio

In `submit()` (lines 297-304) the code now aggregates `get_memory_info()` across one SpansBuffer per flusher process. Each shard-group buffer returns memory stats for every Redis cluster its shards live on, so a cluster that hosts shards in several process groups is counted once per group. The `used / available` ratio is then weighted by how the shards happen to be distributed across processes rather than by actual cluster memory: a nearly-full cluster whose shards fall into only one process group can be diluted below `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` by other, emptier clusters, delaying the 'Pausing consumer due to Redis being full' backpressure until Redis actually evicts data. The per-cluster ServiceMemory results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster/service) before summing.

Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, accumulating zombies

In `_ensure_processes_alive()` the unhealthy process is `kill()`ed and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards()`, but the killed process is never `join()`ed or waited on. A SIGKILLed child becomes a zombie until the parent reaps it; since `process_restarts` is never reset, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS (10) killed processes per process slot can accumulate as zombies over the consumer's lifetime, each also holding an unreaped Kafka producer / Redis connection context. Call `process.join(timeout)` (or at least `process.join()` after kill) before spawning the replacement.

Docstring says 'one process per shard' but default configuration spawns a single process

The class docstring (line 32) states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the new `max_processes` parameter and the CLI option `--flusher-processes` default to 1 (see src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py, default=1), in which case exactly one process handles all shards. The constructor default (`None` -> len(assigned_shards), i.e. per-shard) also disagrees with the CLI default of 1, so behavior differs depending on whether the factory is built via the click command or programmatically. Update the docstring and align the defaults so operators reading either the code or the `--help` text get the same story.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and would double-spawn if ever called

`_create_process_for_shard()` (lines 127-132) is never called anywhere — the restart path goes through `_ensure_processes_alive` -> `_create_process_for_shards` directly. Worse, if someone did call it, it would start a brand-new process for the shard's group without killing or removing the existing process for that group, leaving two processes simultaneously flushing the same shards (duplicate segment production to buffered-segments) and orphaning the old entry in `self.processes`. Remove the method or make it delegate to the kill-and-restart logic in `_ensure_processes_alive`.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The correct approach is to look up each id individually from the returned mapping (e.g. `data = events.get(node_id)`), not to zip two independently ordered sequences.

Adding `String getShortcut();` as an abstract method to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a source- and binary-incompatible change: every existing custom grant-type factory deployed as an extension will fail to compile against the new version, and pre-built jars will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when Keycloak's DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory calls getShortcut() during postInit (which happens at server startup, so the whole server can fail to boot for those deployments). Provide a `default` implementation (e.g. deriving a shortcut from getId() or returning a documented fallback) to preserve compatibility.

It was part of the public SPI surface (this class lives in server-spi-private and is implemented/used by third-party grant extensions), so removing it is a compile-time break for any external code that wrapped or derived a Context. (2) The new `grantType` field is captured once in the constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but `setFormParams(...)` (which external grant implementations can use to swap in re-parsed form params) does not refresh `grantType`. Consequently, when token issuance later reads `context.getGrantType()` in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse and encodes it into the access-token ID, the encoded grant type can be wrong/stale relative to the form params actually in effect, silently corrupting the context metadata this PR introduces.

In getShortcutByGrantType (and getGrantTypeByShortcut), when a grant type is not found in the cached maps, the factory refreshes the cache by blindly doing `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` without checking whether that shortcut is already mapped to a different grant type. If a newly deployed custom grant reuses a shortcut already assigned to another grant (e.g. "ac"), the put overwrites the existing reverse mapping, and from then on tokens containing that shortcut decode to the wrong grant type — data corruption in the token context with no warning. Note the duplicate-shortcut validation only runs once in postInit (line 82), so dynamically deployed/hot-reloaded grants bypass it entirely. The lazy refresh path should detect the collision (existing mapping to a different grant) and fail loudly (log error / throw) instead of overwriting, mirroring the postInit validation.

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext determines the token type via AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session), which evaluates `session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)`. TokenManager.initToken receives the issuing `client` as a parameter, but this path relies on the ambient session-context client being set to the same client; where they diverge (or where the session-context client is null, e.g. token creation invoked from non-request contexts such as backchannel flows or tests), the lookup either returns the wrong client's lightweight setting or throws an NPE. The client used for the lightweight check should be taken from the client session / passed explicitly rather than from session.getContext().

Unit test bypasses factory postInit, so real grant-shortcut wiring is untested

The test's before() method hand-injects a synthetic map (only 'ro', 'cc' and 'na') into the package-private fields instead of running DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit with a real KeycloakSessionFactory, and passes a null session to the provider. As a result, the code paths that production actually exercises — populating maps from the real OAuth2GrantType factories, the postInit duplicate-shortcut validation, and the lazy refresh in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut (which dereferences sessionFactory and would NPE in these tests if hit) — have no coverage. The SQL backend's WatchWriteEvents (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558) initializes its poller's `since` watermark from the *current* latest resource versions at the moment it is called, so every write that occurs while the (potentially long) index build is running is never picked up: it is neither broadcast to Watch subscribers (the Broadcaster/mostRecentRV only see post-start events) nor reflected anywhere. Before this change the watcher was running during index construction, so those events were streamed to clients. The consequence is that any write landing in the startup-indexing window is silently lost from watch streams. The build path already computes the last-read resource version (comment in search.go:375: "when watching, we must add all events since that time"), but nothing uses it; the watcher should be started before or seeded from the index build's RV rather than from latest.

In searchSupport.init, the errgroup closures assign to the captured outer variables `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`, line 190) and increment `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) from multiple concurrent goroutines with no synchronization. This is a data race under the Go memory model. It was mostly latent before because bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized workers behind its whole-function cacheMu lock, but this PR removes that lock specifically to let builds run concurrently, making the race real. Consequences range from torn counters in the "namespaces indexed" span attribute to one goroutine's error return value being overwritten/observed inconsistently by another. Capture local variables inside the closure and use an atomic counter for the total.

Failed Init in NewResourceServer leaks the context and partially started goroutines

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns `nil, err` on failure, but never calls s.cancel() on the error path. If any stage of Init fails partway (e.g., lifecycle hooks succeed, search init starts its event-consumer goroutine, then initWatcher fails), the server object is discarded while the cancelable context and any goroutines spawned during partial initialization keep running. Notably, the searchSupport watch goroutine (search.go:207-213) consumes from the events channel on a context.Background() with no shutdown path at all, so it polls and processes events forever for a server that was never returned to the caller. Call s.cancel() (and ideally give the search watch goroutine a stop mechanism) before returning the error.

The test now skips unconditionally for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres ("test not working with postgres in Drone"), which means the storage server target and the addStorageServerToConfig postgres branch (db_host/db_name/db_user/db_pass keys, lines 75-79) get no CI coverage at all — that configuration code can silently rot. false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() permanently kills the factory-owned queue pool; any Kafka rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and calls queue.shutdown() on every work queue. However, the queue_pool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and shared by every strategy the factory builds. Arroyo's StreamProcessor tears down the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions() again on every rebalance/partition reassignment, which is routine in production. After the first rebalance, the new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wraps a pool whose queues are shut down: FixedQueuePool.submit() -> work_queue.put() raises ValueError, which is swallowed by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (line 317), which marks the offset complete so it gets committed. The result is that after any rebalance, every message is silently dropped while offsets advance, i.e. total silent data loss. The pool's lifecycle must be owned by the factory (only shut down in factory.shutdown()), not by each strategy instance.

Failed messages are marked complete and committed, contradicting the documented 'only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee

OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when self.result_processor(...) raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325) does the same when decoding or grouping_fn raises. The class docstring claims 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but the implementation is at-most-once: a message whose handling fails is logged and its offset committed, so it is never retried or DLQ'd. This is a different failure semantic from other arroyo strategies (RunTask/BatchStep propagate errors so the processor can retry), so operators switching modes will silently lose data that used to be retried. Either the docstring/guarantees must be corrected or failures should keep the offset outstanding (or route to a DLQ).

Graceful shutdown does not drain queued items and the commit thread is stopped before draining, so shutdown loses in-flight work boundaries

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker's loop condition ('while not self.shutdown') is checked after each item, so a worker with a backlog exits after its current item, leaving the remaining queued items unprocessed even though q.shutdown(immediate=False) was specifically chosen to allow draining. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335) stops and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining items, so offsets for items completed during the drain are never committed and those messages are re-consumed (and re-processed, possibly non-idempotently) after restart. The shutdown path should let workers drain the queues first (the queue.ShutDown from q.shutdown(immediate=False) already terminates them), and run a final commit pass after draining.

OffsetTracker stalls forever on permanent offset gaps and does an O(offset-range) scan every second

get_committable_offsets() breaks at the first offset not present in all_offsets and only ever commits up to that point, assuming any gap will eventually be filled by a message passed to submit(). But offsets can be permanently absent from the consumer's view - e.g. Kafka transactional control records that librdkafka filters out, or offsets skipped after consumer-group offset expiry - so a gap that never fills blocks all commits for that partition for the life of the process, causing unbounded offset lag and rebalance risk. Additionally, the scan iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) every second; with such a permanent gap the range grows unboundedly (min to max of ever-seen offsets), making each commit tick progressively more expensive. A safer design is to track only the set of outstanding offsets and commit min(outstanding)-1, rather than requiring contiguity.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the documented claim

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after put(), so the arroyo consumer thread keeps fetching and enqueueing messages as fast as Kafka delivers them. If workers fall behind (the exact 'one slow item clogs a queue' scenario the PR is meant to mitigate, now per-queue instead of per-batch), memory grows without bound and consumer lag accumulates invisibly. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The queues should be constructed with a bounded maxsize (queue.put then blocks the arroyo thread, applying real backpressure), or another bound on in-flight messages is needed.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is racy and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation

The test asserts that no commit happens for a partition after a processing failure ('assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets'). But OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so once the 1-second commit tick fires the strategy will commit offset 102 for the partition. The test only passes if it finishes its wait/sleep before the commit thread's next tick, making it timing-dependent and flaky. It also masks the at-most-once data-loss behavior of the finally-block completion (see the worker implementation); either the implementation or the test's expectation needs to be fixed so they agree deterministically.

In test_stats_reporting, 10 items are submitted to a pool whose workers are already running a trivially fast result_processor, and the test immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0; if the workers drain the queue before get_stats() is called, the assertion fails intermittently. Similarly, test_different_groups_distributed asserts all 3 queue indices are hit by 20 hashed group keys; since string hashes are randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), the mapping is effectively random each run and there is a small but real chance (~0.1%) that only 2 of 3 buckets are used, causing an intermittent failure. These assertions should be made deterministic (e.g., block the workers, or assert the index is within range rather than full coverage).

In _commit_loop, the metric 'remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed' is incremented by len(committable), which is the number of partitions in the commit dict, not the number of Kafka offsets advanced. For a busy consumer committing thousands of offsets per tick across a few partitions, the metric dramatically undercounts and its name misleads anyone dashboarding it. It should report the sum of offset deltas (or be renamed to partitions_committed).

Both merge operations (`redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` at lines 47 and 53) omit an AGGREGATE argument, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same span payload exists in both source keys — which happens under Kafka's at-least-once delivery, e.g. a span delivered in one batch lands in the set keyed by its parent while a duplicate delivery in a later batch lands in the merged set — the resulting member's score is the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values. Since the score is the span's end timestamp used to order the zset, this silently doubles the timestamp. The consequences are that zpopmin eviction (which pops the lowest scores) evicts the wrong spans, and the flush-time iteration order no longer reflects chronological order. The previous sunionstore-based code had no score semantics so this was not an issue; the fix is to pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

The script now evicts the lowest-scored (oldest end_timestamp) members whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Unlike the previous behavior — where oversized segments were skipped at flush time with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log — this eviction is completely silent: there is no metric, no log, and no marker on the flushed segment, so the ongoing data loss is invisible to operators. Additionally, if the segment/root span is among the evicted members (possible whenever its end_timestamp is not the maximum, e.g. async traces), the segment is flushed without any root span, so no span gets `is_segment=True`, while the `span-buf:hrs:` key still reads "1" and forces the shorter root timeout. The limit is also hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, diverging from the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config (default 1001), which this PR leaves as a dead, unused parameter in SpansBuffer.__init__ (buffer.py line 150) — so the two limits can drift and the config can no longer be tuned from Python at all.

The loop bound was reduced tenfold and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:{...}` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with a stale `set_span_id`, and line 40 then writes an incorrect redirect mapping for the incoming span — the span is attached to the wrong segment and the trace is silently assembled incorrectly. There is no error signal when the cap is hit (redirect_depth is returned but nothing distinguishes 'resolved' from 'gave up'). Reducing the guarantee 10x needs at least a metric/alert on `redirect_depth == 1000` or a comment explaining why 1000 is safe; neither is present, and the diff gives no reason for the change.

Direct `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` access will crash the consumer on messages that lack the field

process_batch now reads `end_timestamp_precise` with direct dict indexing. The existing consumer test message did not contain this field until this PR added it, which is evidence that messages without the field are representable in the topic (older producers or schema versions, plus any backlog present at deploy time). A KeyError raised inside process_batch propagates out of the RunTask/multiprocessing strategy and kills the consumer, stalling the whole partition — a much worse failure mode than defaulting the score (e.g. `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or 0` or falling back to the message timestamp). If the field is guaranteed by the current schema, that guarantee should at least be stated; the current code makes any pre-upgrade buffered message fatal.

Comment claims negative offsets 'enable efficient reverse pagination' but they break the offset arithmetic in this module

The new comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets enable "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". That is not how the module works: _build_next_values and _build_prev_values compute offsets by adding/subtracting the page limit from the current offset, and consumers of these cursors slice querysets where negative offsets are unsupported (raising errors) or silently misbehave. The comment documents a capability that does not exist anywhere in the codebase and will mislead future maintainers into relying on it.

false_positives.candidate:
Permission denial cache locks in denies for 30s with no invalidation, defeating the new DB fallback for repeat checks

In Check(), once a DB query confirms a deny, the result is written to permDenialCache (line 154) and every subsequent Check for the same (namespace, user, action, resource name, folder) returns deny from the denial cache before the permission cache or the database is ever consulted. This means the new 'requery the DB when cached permissions deny' fallback (the core fix of this PR) only ever runs once per resource: after the first denied check, a permission granted on that exact resource (e.g. an admin shares a dashboard with a user who was just denied, or a permission row commits shortly after a racing check during resource creation) is not honored for up to 30 seconds. There is also no invalidation hook: in the in-proc path the service uses a private LocalCache that Grafana's accesscontrol cache-invalidation on permission changes cannot reach, and in the shared-cache (RegisterRBACAuthZService) path a denial written by one instance blocks all instances. Consider not writing a denial entry when the deny could race with a grant/creation, or invalidating the denial key when a fresh DB query for the same user/action returns an allow (e.g. via a List or another resource's fallback).

permissionCacheUsage metric now conflates denial-cache hits with permission-cache hits and mislabels decisive-but-denying hits as misses

Conversely, when cached permissions are found but checkPermission denies and the request falls through to the DB, the code increments permissionCacheUsage with "false" (line 137) even though the permission cache was hit — a real hit is recorded as a miss. The metric can no longer be used to observe the new DB-fallback path or the denial-cache hit rate, which are exactly the behaviors this PR introduces and would want to monitor in production. Consider separate label values or a distinct metric for the denial cache and for 'cache hit but denied, fell back to DB'.

In-proc authz client cache removal puts a gRPC call plus per-check JSON decode on every access check

For the default (in-proc) mode the client is now built with a NoopCache, so every authorization check in Grafana core — which happens several times per HTTP request on the hottest path — performs an in-proc gRPC roundtrip, and on the server each cache hit requires JSON-unmarshaling the user's full permission scope map (cacheWrap uses encoding/json, and users with many scoped dashboard/folder permissions have large maps). The previous 30s client-side cache absorbed repeated identical checks entirely in memory. Removing it is necessary for the correctness fix (the client cache served stale denies for newly created resources), but a client-side cache that only caches positive responses would preserve most of the benefit without reintroducing the stale-deny bug, since denies would still always reach the server (where the new denial cache provides the fast negative path). Worth measuring the per-request overhead before merging, or implementing positive-only client caching.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No cache re-check after acquiring the write lock; lock held across file I/O and JSON parsing

Once a goroutine that observed a nil cache acquires the exclusive lock, it never re-checks whether another goroutine has already populated the cache. At startup (or after a failed read, when the cache stays nil), N concurrent requests each perform the full manifest read and JSON decode sequentially while holding the write lock, instead of one goroutine doing it and the rest reusing the result. Additionally, the lock is held across `os.Open` + `json.Decode` and, in Dev mode, this happens on every single request, serializing all index-page requests behind each other's disk I/O. Doing the expensive computation first and only taking the lock to publish the result (double-checked locking) would avoid the redundant work and shrink the critical section.

The PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, but the rule later in the same block still styles its `button { background: transparent; border: 0; float: right; }` (line 309). Children of a flex container become flex items and the `float` property is ignored on them, so the button (e.g. the banner/small-action close button) is no longer pushed to the right edge of the row. It will now render immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text, leaving a gap on the right and misplacing the control. The button needs `margin-left: auto` (or the container needs `justify-content: space-between`) to restore right alignment, as was done for `.panel` in header.scss. The same applies to `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270), though there the flex row layout coincidentally produces a similar result.

.panel right-alignment relies on margin-left: auto, which IE10 flexbox does not honor

The new flexbox mixins explicitly target IE10 by emitting `display: -ms-flexbox` / `-ms-flex-align`, but the header's right-hand `.panel` is positioned purely via `margin-left: auto` (the old `float: right` was removed). IE10's flexbox implementation does not support auto margins for main-axis alignment (alignment there must be done with `-ms-flex-pack`), so on IE10 the search/hamburger/user panel will not be pushed to the right edge of the header and will instead sit directly next to the title. Since the whole point of the `-ms-` prefixes in the mixins is to support that browser, `.contents` needs an `-ms-flex-pack: end`-style fallback (or the panel needs a different mechanism) for the layout to hold there.

align-items() mixin omits the -moz-box-align counterpart that flexbox()/order() imply

`flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` and `order()` emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, so the mixin set explicitly claims to support old-Gecko flexbox; but `align-items()` has no `-moz-box-align` line. Any browser that ends up using the `-moz-box` code path (the only one it is given) will get a flex container with no vertical alignment, so `.d-header .contents`, `.small-action`, and the `.badge-wrapper.bullet` would be laid out with the old default (stretch/start) instead of centered/baseline as intended. Either add `-moz-box-align` for symmetry or drop the `-moz-box` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` output, since the two halves of the vendor story currently contradict each other.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' and is therefore dead code

The guard is defined as `def include_website_name` but ActiveModel::Serializers only invokes include methods named `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_card_image_badge?, etc.) follows that convention. Because of the missing '?', this method is never called, so the intended condition (only serialize website_name when the website is present) never takes effect. When a user has no website, the JSON will still contain a `website_name: null` key, and any future restriction logic added to this guard would silently not run.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the primary bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` required by Rails/ActiveModel::Serializers for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue about string concatenation, the core issue is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses untrusted-attribute hiding for TL0 profiles

The serializer registers :website as an untrusted attribute (untrusted_attributes list, lines 105-111), so when a TL0 user's profile is restricted from anonymous viewers (scope.restrict_user_fields?), the raw :website value is omitted from the JSON. The new :website_name attribute, however, is only listed in the plain `attributes` call (line 43) and its guard `include_website_name` (line 153) only checks `website.present?`. As a result, for restricted TL0 profiles the website host plus path (e.g. 'example.com/private-page') is still serialized and rendered on the profile, leaking exactly the information the hide-profiles setting is meant to conceal. It also breaks the template: since :website is omitted, user.hbs renders `<a href="">` (empty href pointing at the current page) with the leaked website_name as the link text. website_name must be added to untrusted_attributes (or its include method must check restrict_user_fields?).

Untrusted-attributes spec not updated for the new website_name attribute

The test at line 11 asserts that a fixed list of untrusted attributes (bio_raw, bio_cooked, bio_excerpt, location, website, profile_background, card_background) is omitted for TL0 users viewed anonymously, but :website_name was not added to that list. Because of this gap the suite passes even though website_name leaks the website host/path for exactly the profiles the setting protects. The spec should assert `expect(json).not_to have_key(:website_name)` in that context, which would have caught the privacy regression introduced by this change.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of exact origin comparison

The resize handler accepts messages when `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is false, i.e. when the message origin appears anywhere as a substring of discourseUrl. That is not an equality check: any origin that happens to occur inside the discourseUrl string (e.g. as part of a path, or a shorter scheme/host prefix in some configurations) is accepted, and e.data.height is used unvalidated. The consequence is limited to resizing the iframe, but the check should compare `e.origin` against the exact expected origin (e.g. the parsed origin of discourseUrl) and the height coerced to a positive integer.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation for postMessage uses `indexOf` (substring matching) instead of an exact comparison, allowing the check to be bypassed.

true_positives.golden_comment: postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated into a JS string literal without escape_javascript

The layout does `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The referer is only validated to have a host equal to embeddable_host; its path/query can contain arbitrary characters (an attacker can send a request with a crafted Referer header directly — no control of a page on the host is needed). The value is placed in a single-quoted JavaScript string with no `j`/escape_javascript; it currently survives only because Rails' HTML escaping converts quotes to `'`, which then appears literally inside the script block, producing an invalid targetOrigin that makes postMessage throw a SyntaxError and breaks iframe resizing for such referers. It should be escaped with escape_javascript (and ideally the exact origin, not the full referer, used as targetOrigin).
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment points out a functional bug where passing the full referrer URL as the targetOrigin in postMessage (instead of just scheme+host+port) causes the message to be dropped. The candidate issue primarily focuses on a missing `escape_javascript` call when interpolating `request.referer` into a JS string literal. However, at the very end, the candidate explicitly mentions: '(and ideally the exact origin, not the full referer, used as targetOrigin)'. While the primary focus of the candidate is JS escaping, it does explicitly identify the exact issue mentioned in the golden comment on the exact same line of code.

false_positives.candidate:
RSS item content imported as raw_html with no sanitization — stored XSS from feed content

poll_feed passes `i.content` (the raw HTML from the feed's content:encoded/body) straight into TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Post#cook then returns the raw string untouched, skipping the normal cooking/sanitizing pipeline, and best.html.erb renders it with `raw post.cooked`. Anyone who can influence the feed's HTML (compromised or malicious feed source at the admin-configured feed_polling_url) gets arbitrary JavaScript executed on the Discourse origin for every viewer, including logged-in staff. The readability path at least whitelists tags/attributes; the feed path has no equivalent. The imported HTML should be run through a sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs that pass the http(s) regex

TopicEmbed.import only gates on `url =~ /^https?:///`, but absolutize_urls then calls `URI(url)` which raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs containing spaces or other invalid characters (e.g. `http://exa mple.com/post` or an unencoded `%zz`). Unlike TopicRetriever#invalid_host?, there is no rescue here, so a single malformed feed link (or a crafted embed_url) raises an unhandled exception. In PollFeed this aborts the remaining feed items; in RetrieveTopic the job fails. The URI parse should be guarded or the URL rejected up front with a full URI parse.

Feed and page fetches use open() with no timeout; a slow source hangs the job and the hourly schedule

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (and `open(url)` in TopicEmbed.import_remote) use Kernel#open with no read/open timeout. The scheduled job has `retry: false` and is also invoked synchronously from TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve on a user-triggered retrieve, so a hanging or very slow feed server blocks a Sidekiq worker indefinitely and stalls subsequent scheduled runs. open-uri should be given `open_timeout`/`read_timeout` (or a job-level timeout).

setnx/expire are not atomic; a crash between them permanently disables retrieval for a URL

retrieved_recently? performs `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies between the two calls (or the expire fails), the key exists with no TTL and the URL is considered 'recently retrieved' forever — the embed will never be fetched again through the throttled path, leaving the loading page reloading every 30 seconds indefinitely. A single SET key 1 EX 60 NX (or a Lua script) should be used instead.

embed_url column is varchar(255); real URLs (plus the appended footer) can exceed it

The embed_url column is a Rails `string`, i.e. varchar(255) on PostgreSQL, with a NOT NULL constraint. Web page URLs frequently exceed 255 characters, and TopicEmbed.import additionally embeds the URL twice (href and text) into the post body; an over-long feed link will make the INSERT fail with 'value too long for type character varying(255)', aborting the import. The column should be text (or a larger limit) to match how URLs are stored elsewhere.

`force: true` added to an existing migration will drop an already-created top_topics table

This PR changes the previously shipped CreateTopTopics migration to `create_table :top_topics, force: true`. With force: true, create_table drops the table if it already exists; any environment that already ran the original migration and then re-runs it (db:migrate:redo, rebuilding from migrations rather than schema.rb) will silently lose all top_topics data. If the change was needed for test databases, it should be made in a separate migration or the test schema rebuilt, not by editing a released migration.

Only Gemfile_rails4.lock was updated; the default (Rails 3) lockfile is missing the new gems

The PR adds ruby-readability and simple-rss to the Gemfile and updates Gemfile_rails4.lock, but the repository's dual-boot setup (see the Bundler monkey patch at the top of the Gemfile) uses the default Gemfile.lock when booting in Rails 3 mode (`RAILS3` set), which per the diff was not regenerated. Any Rails 3-mode CI run or deployment will fail to resolve the new dependencies (TopicEmbed/poll_feed require them at runtime), so the Rails 3 lockfile needs the corresponding entries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the width/height variant

The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first, so the width/height variant is dead code. Any existing caller that invokes `downsize(from, to, width, height)` will now have its `height` argument bound to the `opts` parameter; when `optimize` evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer it raises `TypeError (no implicit conversion of Integer into Hash-like)`. Either remove the old signature entirely or rename/merge the two methods so the four-argument form still works.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the `downsize` method is defined twice, causing the second definition (taking `dimensions`) to override the first definition (taking `max_width` and `max_height`), which renders the first unreachable and breaks existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB limit ignores admin-configured max upload sizes

validateUploadedFile now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, and the 413 handler at line 246 similarly hardcodes 10 MB instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. This silently disables the `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` site settings on the client: admins who set a lower limit will see users attempting uploads up to 10 MB (which then fail server-side with a confusing error for attachments), and admins who set a higher limit will get an incorrect 'file too large' rejection in the browser. This looks like leftover debug/test code (the PR description is 'Test 1') and should be reverted to read the settings.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: hardcoding `10 * 1024` instead of reading `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` (and the similar change in the 413 handler), which causes the client-side limit to ignore admin-configured settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop can never bring very large images under the limit and ignores downsize failures

The retry loop runs at most 5 iterations, each downsizing to '80%', so the best possible reduction is to 0.8^5 ≈ 33% of the original size. An image more than ~3x `max_image_size_kb` will still exceed the limit when the loop exits, and the oversized file is then passed to `Upload.create_for`, which will reject it — the user waits through 5 ImageMagim/ImageOptim passes only to get the same failure the feature was supposed to prevent. Additionally, the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is never checked: if conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image or ImageMagick policy limits), the loop blindly retries five times and may hand a truncated/corrupted tempfile to `Upload.create_for`. The loop should either compute the exact target percentage needed in one pass or check the downsize result and bail out with a clear error.

allow_animation option never applies to uploads because animated-GIF detection relies on the file extension

The controller passes `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but `OptimizedImage.optimize` (optimized_image.rb line 155) only chooses the animated code path when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The `from` path here is an uploaded/action-dispatched tempfile (RackMultipart-* or discourse-upload-*), which never ends in `.gif`, so animated GIFs are always processed through `convert #{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame. Even on sites with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, every oversized animated GIF upload is silently stripped down to a single static frame — permanent loss of the original animation since the tempfile is downsized in place.

Hardcoded 10MB download cap regresses API uploads for sites with larger configured limits

The API URL-download path changed `FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. On sites where an admin has raised `max_image_size_kb` above 10240 KB, remote images larger than 10 MB can no longer be fetched via the API at all (the download silently returns nil due to `rescue nil`, leading to a confusing failure downstream), even though such uploads were previously allowed. The cap should be derived from the setting (e.g. `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` plus some headroom to allow downsizing), not hardcoded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TopicsController#unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when the user has no TopicUser record

In the new `unsubscribe` action, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil (any logged-in user can visit /t/<any topic>/unsubscribe for a topic they have never viewed, posted in, or been emailed about — the URL is trivially guessable since it is just the topic URL plus /unsubscribe). The code then calls `tu.notification_level` on nil, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500. The action should create/normalize the record via `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` like `set_notifications` does, which also correctly sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` and publishes the MessageBus `notification_level_change` event that the direct `tu.save!` path skips.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `tu` can be `nil` when no `TopicUser` record is found, causing a crash (nil pointer / NoMethodError) when methods are subsequently called on `tu`.

false_positives.candidate: State-changing GET endpoint is vulnerable to CSRF and accidental triggering The new `unsubscribe` action mutates the user's notification level on a GET request. A logged-in user's browser can be made to hit this URL cross-site (e.g. an `` on an attacker page sends session cookies), silently muting or un-muting topics for the victim. Additionally, because the handler *toggles* state (watching/tracking -> regular, otherwise -> muted), any repeated visit — a page refresh, browser pre-render/prefetch of the email link, or a scanner following links in an open session — flips the user's notification level again, potentially re-subscribing someone who just unsubscribed. State changes should be made via a POST endpoint (the email link can go to a page with a button, or use a per-user token), not on GET.

unsubscribe_link locale now requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking any email builder caller that doesn't pass it

The `unsubscribe_link` translation was changed to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `Email::MessageBuilder` merges its opts into template_args, so any caller using `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will now raise `I18n::MissingInterpolationData` when building the body (`body << I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`) or the HTML part, and the email will fail to send. This is an undocumented new contract on the MessageBuilder API — nothing enforces or documents that `unsubscribe_url` must accompany `add_unsubscribe_link`, so plugins or future mailers that only pass `add_unsubscribe_link` will break. The builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. fall back to the preferences URL) or omit that sentence when it is absent, and this requirement needs a test.

Unsubscribe toggle does not actually unsubscribe watching/tracking users, contradicting the email text

The controller demotes watching/tracking users only to `regular` on the first click. At the `regular` notification level the user still receives notifications when they are replied to, mentioned, or quoted, yet the email footer added in this PR says "To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here" and the client page says "You will stop receiving notifications for <title>". A watching user who clicks the unsubscribe link in the email will keep getting reply/mention emails for that topic. If the intent is a toggle, the messaging is wrong; if the intent is unsubscribe, the level should go to `muted` (or the UI should make the choice explicit before mutating).

No tests for the new TopicsController#unsubscribe behavior

The new `unsubscribe` action implements toggle semantics, slug-mismatch 301 redirects, permission handling, and TopicUser mutation, but no request/controller specs were added for any of it (the only test touched in the PR is the message_builder spec, which merely adds an `unsubscribe_url` option without asserting the topic link appears in the body or List-Unsubscribe header). Given the reachable nil crash and the CSRF-prone GET noted above, this endpoint needs specs covering: user with no TopicUser record, watching vs regular vs muted starting levels, wrong-slug redirect, and inaccessible topic.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' syntax is macOS-only and fails on GNU/Linux

The script uses `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|"` which is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed (standard on Linux CI/dev containers), the empty-string argument after `-i` is not treated as an in-place suffix, so sed interprets `''` as the script and the substitution expression as a filename, causing the command to fail with an error and leaving `.env` unmodified (or worse, running the wrong edit). Use a portable approach (e.g. `sed -i.bak` + remove the backup, or detect the OS), since this script is committed to the shared repo.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-process SpansBuffer memory info double-counts Redis clusters, skewing the hard-backpressure ratio

In `submit()` (lines 297-304) the code now aggregates `get_memory_info()` across one SpansBuffer per flusher process. Each shard-group buffer returns memory stats for every Redis cluster its shards live on, so a cluster that hosts shards in several process groups is counted once per group. The `used / available` ratio is then weighted by how the shards happen to be distributed across processes rather than by actual cluster memory: a nearly-full cluster whose shards fall into only one process group can be diluted below `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` by other, emptier clusters, delaying the 'Pausing consumer due to Redis being full' backpressure until Redis actually evicts data. In `_ensure_processes_alive()` the unhealthy process is `kill()`ed and a replacement is immediately spawned via `_create_process_for_shards()`, but the killed process is never `join()`ed or waited on. A SIGKILLed child becomes a zombie until the parent reaps it; since `process_restarts` is never reset, up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS (10) killed processes per process slot can accumulate as zombies over the consumer's lifetime, each also holding an unreaped Kafka producer / Redis connection context. Call `process.join(timeout)` (or at least `process.join()` after kill) before spawning the replacement.

The class docstring (line 32) states 'Creates one process per shard for parallel processing', but the new `max_processes` parameter and the CLI option `--flusher-processes` default to 1 (see src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py, default=1), in which case exactly one process handles all shards. It was part of the public SPI surface (this class lives in server-spi-private and is implemented/used by third-party grant extensions), so removing it is a compile-time break for any external code that wrapped or derived a Context. (2) The new `grantType` field is captured once in the constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but `setFormParams(...)` (which external grant implementations can use to swap in re-parsed form params) does not refresh `grantType`. In getShortcutByGrantType (and getGrantTypeByShortcut), when a grant type is not found in the cached maps, the factory refreshes the cache by blindly doing `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` without checking whether that shortcut is already mapped to a different grant type. If a newly deployed custom grant reuses a shortcut already assigned to another grant (e.g. "ac"), the put overwrites the existing reverse mapping, and from then on tokens containing that shortcut decode to the wrong grant type — data corruption in the token context with no warning. Note the duplicate-shortcut validation only runs once in postInit (line 82), so dynamically deployed/hot-reloaded grants bypass it entirely. The lazy refresh path should detect the collision (existing mapping to a different grant) and fail loudly (log error / throw) instead of overwriting, mirroring the postInit validation.

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext determines the token type via AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session), which evaluates `session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)`. TokenManager.initToken receives the issuing `client` as a parameter, but this path relies on the ambient session-context client being set to the same client; where they diverge (or where the session-context client is null, e.g. token creation invoked from non-request contexts such as backchannel flows or tests), the lookup either returns the wrong client's lightweight setting or throws an NPE. The client used for the lightweight check should be taken from the client session / passed explicitly rather than from session.getContext().

The test's before() method hand-injects a synthetic map (only 'ro', 'cc' and 'na') into the package-private fields instead of running DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit with a real KeycloakSessionFactory, and passes a null session to the provider. The contract for what a storage should store (raw vs hashed, and in which JSON shape so that RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel can parse it in getCredential()) is undefined; a provider that naively persists the array as credentialData will break createFromCredentialModel with a parse error.

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the entire function, which (coarsely) guaranteed that only one build per key could run at a time and that GetIndex would block rather than return nil mid-build. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. The caller, searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:287), does a check-then-build with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO comment admits this: "We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key... simple mutex not great"). For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory, which fails or corrupts the on-disk index; for in-memory indexes the build runs twice, IndexedKinds/IndexTenants metrics are double-counted, and the index object that loses the cache-map race is the one that handleEvent may keep writing watch events into, so those updates silently disappear from searches. A per-key singleflight/mutex is needed to preserve the exclusion the old lock provided.

false_positives.candidate:

Init previously called s.initWatcher() before s.search.init(); it now runs the search index build first and only starts the event watcher afterwards. The SQL backend's WatchWriteEvents (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558) initializes its poller's `since` watermark from the *current* latest resource versions at the moment it is called, so every write that occurs while the (potentially long) index build is running is never picked up: it is neither broadcast to Watch subscribers (the Broadcaster/mostRecentRV only see post-start events) nor reflected anywhere. Before this change the watcher was running during index construction, so those events were streamed to clients. The consequence is that any write landing in the startup-indexing window is silently lost from watch streams. The build path already computes the last-read resource version (comment in search.go:375: "when watching, we must add all events since that time"), but nothing uses it; the watcher should be started before or seeded from the index build's RV rather than from latest.

In searchSupport.init, the errgroup closures assign to the captured outer variables `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`, line 190) and increment `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) from multiple concurrent goroutines with no synchronization. This is a data race under the Go memory model. It was mostly latent before because bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized workers behind its whole-function cacheMu lock, but this PR removes that lock specifically to let builds run concurrently, making the race real. Consequences range from torn counters in the "namespaces indexed" span attribute to one goroutine's error return value being overwritten/observed inconsistently by another. Capture local variables inside the closure and use an atomic counter for the total.

If any stage of Init fails partway (e.g., lifecycle hooks succeed, search init starts its event-consumer goroutine, then initWatcher fails), the server object is discarded while the cancelable context and any goroutines spawned during partial initialization keep running. Notably, the searchSupport watch goroutine (search.go:207-213) consumes from the events channel on a context.Background() with no shutdown path at all, so it polls and processes events forever for a server that was never returned to the caller. The pool's lifecycle must be owned by the factory (only shut down in factory.shutdown()), not by each strategy instance.

Failed messages are marked complete and committed, contradicting the documented 'only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee

OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when self.result_processor(...) raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325) does the same when decoding or grouping_fn raises. The class docstring claims 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but the implementation is at-most-once: a message whose handling fails is logged and its offset committed, so it is never retried or DLQ'd. This is a different failure semantic from other arroyo strategies (RunTask/BatchStep propagate errors so the processor can retry), so operators switching modes will silently lose data that used to be retried. Either the docstring/guarantees must be corrected or failures should keep the offset outstanding (or route to a DLQ).

Graceful shutdown does not drain queued items and the commit thread is stopped before draining, so shutdown loses in-flight work boundaries

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker's loop condition ('while not self.shutdown') is checked after each item, so a worker with a backlog exits after its current item, leaving the remaining queued items unprocessed even though q.shutdown(immediate=False) was specifically chosen to allow draining. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335) stops and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining items, so offsets for items completed during the drain are never committed and those messages are re-consumed (and re-processed, possibly non-idempotently) after restart. The shutdown path should let workers drain the queues first (the queue.ShutDown from q.shutdown(immediate=False) already terminates them), and run a final commit pass after draining.

OffsetTracker stalls forever on permanent offset gaps and does an O(offset-range) scan every second

get_committable_offsets() breaks at the first offset not present in all_offsets and only ever commits up to that point, assuming any gap will eventually be filled by a message passed to submit(). But offsets can be permanently absent from the consumer's view - e.g. Kafka transactional control records that librdkafka filters out, or offsets skipped after consumer-group offset expiry - so a gap that never fills blocks all commits for that partition for the life of the process, causing unbounded offset lag and rebalance risk. Additionally, the scan iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) every second; with such a permanent gap the range grows unboundedly (min to max of ever-seen offsets), making each commit tick progressively more expensive. A safer design is to track only the set of outstanding offsets and commit min(outstanding)-1, rather than requiring contiguity.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the documented claim

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after put(), so the arroyo consumer thread keeps fetching and enqueueing messages as fast as Kafka delivers them. If workers fall behind (the exact 'one slow item clogs a queue' scenario the PR is meant to mitigate, now per-queue instead of per-batch), memory grows without bound and consumer lag accumulates invisibly. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The queues should be constructed with a bounded maxsize (queue.put then blocks the arroyo thread, applying real backpressure), or another bound on in-flight messages is needed.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is racy and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation

The test asserts that no commit happens for a partition after a processing failure ('assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets'). But OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so once the 1-second commit tick fires the strategy will commit offset 102 for the partition. The test only passes if it finishes its wait/sleep before the commit thread's next tick, making it timing-dependent and flaky. It also masks the at-most-once data-loss behavior of the finally-block completion (see the worker implementation); either the implementation or the test's expectation needs to be fixed so they agree deterministically.

test_stats_reporting races on queue depth and test_different_groups_distributed can flake under hash randomization

In test_stats_reporting, 10 items are submitted to a pool whose workers are already running a trivially fast result_processor, and the test immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0; if the workers drain the queue before get_stats() is called, the assertion fails intermittently. Similarly, test_different_groups_distributed asserts all 3 queue indices are hit by 20 hashed group keys; since string hashes are randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), the mapping is effectively random each run and there is a small but real chance (~0.1%) that only 2 of 3 buckets are used, causing an intermittent failure. These assertions should be made deterministic (e.g., block the workers, or assert the index is within range rather than full coverage).

'offsets_committed' metric counts partitions, not offsets

In _commit_loop, the metric 'remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed' is incremented by len(committable), which is the number of partitions in the commit dict, not the number of Kafka offsets advanced. For a busy consumer committing thousands of offsets per tick across a few partitions, the metric dramatically undercounts and its name misleads anyone dashboarding it. It should report the sum of offset deltas (or be renamed to partitions_committed).

When the same span payload exists in both source keys — which happens under Kafka's at-least-once delivery, e.g. a span delivered in one batch lands in the set keyed by its parent while a duplicate delivery in a later batch lands in the merged set — the resulting member's score is the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values. Since the score is the span's end timestamp used to order the zset, this silently doubles the timestamp. The consequences are that zpopmin eviction (which pops the lowest scores) evicts the wrong spans, and the flush-time iteration order no longer reflects chronological order. The previous sunionstore-based code had no score semantics so this was not an issue; the fix is to pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

There is no error signal when the cap is hit (redirect_depth is returned but nothing distinguishes 'resolved' from 'gave up'). In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup registrations use `testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove` with the hard-coded string "alias" instead of the actual aliases that were created ("idp-alias-" + i at line 381, and "idp-alias-20" at line 425). None of the 20+ identity providers created by the test are ever removed, so they leak into subsequent tests in the realm (any test that counts or lists realm IDPs will see stale brokers). Additionally, at cleanup time the registered runnable calls remove() on the non-existent "alias" resource, which returns 404 and can make the cleanup itself fail. The correct call is `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("idp-alias-" + i)::remove)` (and `get("idp-alias-20")` for the later one). Note the same copy-pasted defect exists at line 303 in testCacheIDPByOrg, which suggests the bug was copied from there.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same cleanup bug: using the literal alias "alias" instead of the created identity provider alias "idp-alias-" + i. Its additional discussion of leaked test data and cleanup failures does not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate evaluates the login predicate on the organization-wrapped model, so invalidation can be wrongly skipped

In update(), the "original" model passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate comes from getById(), which returns a model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to return false whenever the linked organization (or the organization provider) is disabled, regardless of the IDP's own enabled flag. The login caches, however, are populated purely from intrinsic IDP properties (enabled, linkOnly, hideOnLogin, brokerPublic, organizationId) — an IDP belonging to a disabled org is still stored in the cached login lists. Scenario: (1) an org-linked, public, enabled IDP is cached in the login list; (2) the organization is disabled (this does not touch the IDP, so no cache invalidation); (3) an admin updates the IDP to disabled or non-public — the wrapped original fails getLoginPredicate() (isEnabled()=false due to the disabled org) and the updated model also fails, so registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate returns early and the login caches are NOT invalidated even though the IDP is in them and no longer qualifies; (4) when the org is re-enabled, getForLogin serves the stale cached list containing an IDP that is disabled/non-public, violating the SPI contract that getForLogin returns only IDPs available for login. The impact on the login page is currently masked because OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean re-filters, but any other consumer of getForLogin gets stale results. Fix: compute the predicate on the raw delegate model (e.g. idpDelegate.getById(...)) instead of the wrapped one, so the skip-invalidation decision depends only on intrinsic IDP properties.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() is dead logic that always returns false regardless of the feature toggle

The function `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` but then returns `false` in both branches of the following `if`, so the flag check has no effect whatsoever. While the net effect (always disabled) is the security intent of this PR, the code reads as if the feature flag were consulted, which will mislead future maintainers who may 'fix' or extend it. If SQL expressions are meant to be permanently disabled, the function should simply be removed and the call site should unconditionally reject the query; if the flag is meant to matter, the logic is wrong. As written, the `FlagSqlExpressions` feature toggle silently no-ops, and the only user-visible signal is the confusing error at the call site.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same flawed logic in enableSqlExpressions: it returns false in every branch, so the feature toggle has no effect and SQL expressions are unconditionally disabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is wrong/misleading and is not a proper bad-request error

When a user submits a SQL expression query, they now get `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`. This message is inaccurate: the feature was implemented and has now been deliberately removed/disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). Users who had the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle enabled will get a message that sounds like a transient bug rather than an intentional removal, generating support noise. Additionally, unlike other invalid-query errors in this file's sibling commands (e.g. `errutil.BadRequest("sql-missing-query", ...)` in sql_command.go), this is a bare `fmt.Errorf`, so the API will likely surface it as a 500 internal server error instead of a 400 for what is invalid user input. The message should clearly state that SQL expressions are no longer available and be returned as a bad-request error.

UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not guarded by the same disable check as ReadQuery

The disable logic was only added to the new `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` path (reader.go, QueryTypeSQL case). The older `UnmarshalSQLCommand` entry point (used when raw nodes are unmarshalled from the legacy query format) still constructs a `SQLCommand` without checking whether SQL expressions are disabled. It currently fails anyway, but only as a side effect: `NewSQLCommand` calls `sql.TablesList`, which calls the stub `DB.RunCommands` that returns "not implemented", and that error is surfaced to the user as `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql", "error reading SQL command")` — an error code and message that misrepresent the real cause (feature disabled, not invalid SQL). If the stub DB is ever given a real implementation, this unguarded path would silently re-enable SQL expressions. Both entry points should share a single explicit guard.

NoData branch in Execute is dead code — TableData assignment unconditionally overwrites it

In `SQLCommand.Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values` to a `mathexp.NoData` value, but immediately after the `if` block, `rsp.Values` is unconditionally reassigned to `mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}}`. The NoData result can therefore never be observed, so downstream consumers that distinguish empty frames from NoData (e.g. alerting) get a TableData with zero rows instead. This is a pre-existing bug in a function this PR modifies, and it is worth fixing or removing the dead branch while the function is being touched (it also becomes entirely unreachable now that `QueryFramesInto` always returns an error).

No tests added or updated to cover the new "SQL expressions disabled" behavior

This PR changes user-visible behavior for the `sql` query type (it now always fails, both via the reader path with the new error and via `UnmarshalSQLCommand` which now fails in `sql.TablesList`), yet no test files are included in the change set. There is no test asserting that a SQL expression query returns an error, that the error is a bad-request rather than a 500, or that the legacy `UnmarshalSQLCommand` path is also blocked. Any existing tests covering SQL expression parsing/execution (in pkg/expr and pkg/expr/sql) would exercise the new stub DB and either fail or need updating — none are modified here. Given this is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264, regression tests proving both entry points reject SQL expressions are important to prevent accidental re-enablement.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No cache re-check after acquiring the write lock; lock held across file I/O and JSON parsing

Once a goroutine that observed a nil cache acquires the exclusive lock, it never re-checks whether another goroutine has already populated the cache. At startup (or after a failed read, when the cache stays nil), N concurrent requests each perform the full manifest read and JSON decode sequentially while holding the write lock, instead of one goroutine doing it and the rest reusing the result. Additionally, the lock is held across `os.Open` + `json.Decode` and, in Dev mode, this happens on every single request, serializing all index-page requests behind each other's disk I/O. Doing the expensive computation first and only taking the lock to publish the result (double-checked locking) would avoid the redundant work and shrink the critical section.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, which is the same incomplete double-checked locking issue described by the golden comment. Its additional concerns about holding the lock during I/O do not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Mutex guards only the cache pointer, not the shared EntryPointAssets object handed to callers

The new RWMutex protects reads/writes of the `entryPointAssetsCache` variable, but in non-Dev mode `GetWebAssets` still returns the *same* `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` instance to every concurrent request. That type is mutable: it has exported fields (`JSFiles`, `Dark`, `Light`) and a mutating method `SetContentDeliveryURL`. If any caller (now or in the future) mutates the returned value — e.g. calls `SetContentDeliveryURL` or appends to `JSFiles` — that write races with all other goroutines reading the same object, reproducing exactly the class of bug this PR is meant to fix. To fully close the race, return a copy of the cached value, or make the DTO immutable.

No regression test for the fixed data race

The PR fixes a data race on shared global state but adds no test that would have caught it, so a future refactor could silently reintroduce it. A small test calling `GetWebAssets` concurrently from several goroutines (run under `go test -race`) would lock the fix in, and would also fail on the pre-PR code, demonstrating the bug.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
