true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without documentation or rationale

The cleanup service ticker was changed from time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10) to time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1). This is not mentioned in the PR description, which only describes the annotation delete restructuring. The consequence is that ALL cleanup jobs (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, user invites, short URLs, query history row-limit enforcement, annotation cleanup) now run 10x more often on every Grafana instance, increasing background database load — ironically increasing lock contention with foreground writes, which is the problem this PR is meant to reduce. Combined with the 9-minute per-run timeout in clean(), cleanup work can now effectively run back-to-back. Either this change is unintentional and should be reverted, or it needs to be called out in the PR description and release notes with justification.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker interval changing from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting increased database load and contention from more frequent cleanup execution. The candidate adds details but addresses the same underlying concern.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only guards SQLite and keys off config, not actual ID count

deleteByIDs special-cases only SQLite (r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999) to inline IDs into the SQL, on the assumption that a DELETE with N `?` placeholders is otherwise safe. Other backends have their own placeholder/statement-size limits (e.g. MySQL prepared statements cap at 65,535 placeholders); with annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size configured above such a limit, every batch of the cleanup job will now fail permanently, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE worked for any batch size. The guard should be based on len(ids) against per-dialect limits rather than the configured batch size on SQLite only. Also, the comment claims "SQLite has a parameter limit of 999" while the new test name states the limit is 32767 for SQLite >= 3.32.0 — the comment and code disagree with the test's stated rationale.

Deadlock fix is only exercised on SQLite; no MySQL/Postgres coverage

The PR fixes a MySQL-specific deadlock (grafana/grafana#64979), but all tests in this file use db.InitTestDB(t), which defaults to SQLite. The new code paths (fetchIDs + deleteByIDs, the SQLite ID-inlining branch, the batched untilDoneOrCancelled loop) are only validated against SQLite semantics; in particular the inline-ID branch at deleteByIDs is exercised only via the SQLite test, and no test verifies that the split statements actually avoid the deadlock under concurrent inserts on MySQL. There is also no test for the non-SQLite placeholder path with a large batch size. A MySQL integration test (or at least a concurrency test simulating interleaved inserts during cleanup) is needed to validate the fix the PR claims to deliver.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete success path records the object name as the 'kind' metric label

In `Delete`, the success path calls `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`, passing the object's `name` where every other call in the file passes `options.Kind`. This creates high-cardinality metric labels (one per object name) on this one code path and makes the 'kind' label inconsistent between success and failure (`options.Kind`) for the same method, breaking dashboards/alerts that aggregate by kind.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same metrics inconsistency: Delete passes the object name instead of options.Kind to recordStorageDuration, unlike other calls.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes are canceled as soon as the request context ends

The goroutines that write to LegacyStorage (in Create at line 50-57, Delete at line 108-114, Update at line 134-141, and DeleteCollection at line 161-167) derive their timeout context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. The request-scoped `ctx` is canceled by the apiserver as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which for these fire-and-forget goroutines is typically before the legacy write even starts. The legacy write will then fail almost immediately with 'context canceled' (or the custom timeout cause), so mode 3 effectively never replicates writes to legacy storage in production. The timeout context must be derived from a non-cancelable context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or context.Background()), otherwise the whole point of dual-writing to legacy as a 'safe measure' is defeated.

Legacy Update now receives raw objInfo, causing resourceVersion conflicts and store divergence

The previous implementation wrapped the object before passing it to `d.Legacy.Update` (via `updateWrapper`), so legacy received the already-computed updated object. The new code passes the original `objInfo` to the legacy store. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` typically carries the resourceVersion/preconditions from the client request, which was read from unified storage. The legacy store has its own, different resourceVersion for the object, so the legacy update will frequently fail with a conflict (or apply a stale base object), leaving the legacy copy silently divergent from unified storage. Since legacy write errors are swallowed (only a metric bool), operators have no way to notice this drift. If raw objInfo is intentional, the conflict handling at least needs to be addressed.

Storage failures are recorded as legacy-storage metrics

In `Create` (line 45) and `Update` (line 129), when the write to unified Storage fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` — recording a *legacy* duration using the *storage* start time. This pollutes the legacy-write-duration metric with storage failures and makes the storage error rate invisible (the storage duration for the failed call is never recorded in these paths). The calls should be `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

DeleteCollection records the legacy write under the storage metric

The async goroutine in `DeleteCollection` calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` for the legacy write. It should call `recordLegacyDuration`, as the other write methods do. As written, legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to the unified storage metric, and the legacy metric silently shows nothing, which will mislead anyone monitoring dual-write health during migration.

Legacy write errors in the async goroutines are never logged

In all four write paths, the error returned by the legacy store (e.g. `errObjectSt` at line 55, `err` at lines 112, 139, 165) is reduced to a boolean for the metric and then discarded — there is no `log.Error(...)` call in any of the goroutines. Because mode 3 intentionally treats legacy as a safety net, silent failures mean operators cannot distinguish 'legacy is in sync' from 'every legacy write is failing' without scraping metric internals. The error should be logged with the object name/kind so divergence can be investigated.

Mode 3 tests never assert that the async legacy write happens

The defining new behavior of mode 3 is 'write to unified storage, then asynchronously write to legacy'. None of the mode 3 tests assert that `Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection` are actually invoked after a successful storage write — there is no `m.AssertExpectations`, no wait/poll for the goroutine, and no assertion like `ls.AssertCalled(t, "Create", ...)`. The legacy mock expectations that are set up (e.g. lines 30-32, 313-315) are never verified. Additionally, because the legacy calls run in unmanaged goroutines, a testify mock may be invoked concurrently with (or after) the test body, which is a latent data race / flake. The core contract of this PR is therefore untested at the unit level.

Mode 3 integration subtests will be flaky: legacy API is checked immediately after async legacy writes

The new mode 3 subtests (lines 132 and 191) reuse `doPlaylistTests`, which asserts immediately after k8s writes that the legacy API returns the same data (e.g. `getFromBothAPIs` at lines 547 and 565, including `require.Equal(t, updated.GetResourceVersion(), out.GetResourceVersion())`, and the legacy list comparison at lines 523-531). In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous with no synchronization, so these assertions race the background goroutine and will intermittently fail (stale interval/title, missing item, or not-found from the legacy endpoint). These subtests need a retry/poll helper for the legacy-side checks, or the assertions must tolerate eventual consistency.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in the rules list

In FilterViewResults, the 'grafana' switch branch renders <GrafanaRuleListItem rule={rule} groupIdentifier={...} ... /> without passing the `key` prop. The old <GrafanaRuleLoader> had `key={key}`, and the sibling branches ('datasource' and the default) still pass `key={key}`. The KeyedRuleWithOrigin type comment explicitly states the artificial key exists 'to prevent key duplication' in the rule list. Without a key, React falls back to index-based reconciliation, which can misassociate state (e.g. open dropdowns, drawers) with the wrong rule when items are added/removed during infinite scroll or polling, and produces duplicate-index warnings. Pass `key={key}` to GrafanaRuleListItem.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing React key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in a rendered list and the resulting reconciliation issues when list items change order.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence notifications menu item does nothing in the new Grafana rule list

The 'Silence notifications' menu item is shown whenever `canSilence` is true, and `canSilence` can now be satisfied purely via the new `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` path (which only needs the prom rule). However, the drawer that the click handler opens is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`, where `rule` is the ruler rule. In the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem -> RuleActionsButtons) no ruler rule is passed, so `rule` is undefined, the condition is always false, and the SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer never renders. Users with silence permission see the menu item, click it, and nothing happens. Either pass the prom rule to the drawer or gate the menu item on the drawer actually being openable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: list views pass only the Prom rule to RuleActionsButtons, allowing the silence menu item to appear via Grafana Prom abilities, while the drawer still requires a Grafana Ruler rule. Clicking the item therefore toggles state without rendering the drawer.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete (and Pause) menu items can never render in the ruler-less list view despite abilities being computed for them

AlertRuleMenu now computes `canDelete` (and `canPause`) as an OR of the ruler-rule ability and the new grafana prom-rule ability, specifically so the menu works in the alert list view where no ruler rule is fetched. But the render conditions still require the ruler rule: the Delete item is `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}` (line 165) and the Pause item is `{canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...}` (line 123). Since RuleActionsButtons passes `rulerRule={rule}` with `rule === undefined` in the new list, Delete and Pause silently disappear from the list view even for users with AlertingRuleDelete/Update permissions — a regression from the previous list where ruler rules were fetched and these actions were available. The grafana-based canDelete/canPause computations are dead code as rendered. Either remove the rulerRule gate and make the handlers work from the prom-rule identifier, or drop the grafana ability path for these actions.

Test codifies the missing Delete action instead of catching the regression

The test 'should render correct menu actions when More button is clicked' grants AlertingRuleDelete (and AlertingRuleUpdate) permissions via grantUserPermissions and setFolderAccessControl, yet asserts `menuItems.length` is exactly 4 (silence, copy link, duplicate, export) with no Delete item. This locks in the regression where Delete (and Pause) are unreachable in the ruler-less list view, and the comment 'all 4 menu actions should be available' contradicts the granted permissions. The test should assert that Delete is present when the user has delete permission, and there is no test covering clicking 'Silence notifications' (which would reveal the drawer never opens) or the pause action.

Removed ruler reconciliation drops transient Creating/Deleting states

GrafanaGroupLoader previously merged the Prometheus and Ruler group responses: ruler-only rules (just created, not yet propagated to Prometheus) rendered as 'Creating', and prom-only rules (deleted in the ruler, not yet propagated) rendered as a read-only 'Deleting' item. Now only `promResponse.data.groups.at(0)?.rules` is rendered. Consequences: (1) a newly created rule is invisible in the list until Prometheus propagation completes, with no feedback; (2) a rule the user just deleted still renders as a fully normal, active list item with an Edit button (and copy-link/export) that operate on a rule that no longer exists in the ruler, producing failing actions and confusion. If eventual consistency is now guaranteed, that should be validated; otherwise the eventual-consistency handling needs to be preserved.

Rule view link no longer carries returnTo, breaking back-navigation to the list

The deleted GrafanaRuleLoader/GrafanaRuleListItem built the rule href as createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo }) using createReturnTo(), so navigating to the rule view preserved the list context for the back/return navigation. The new GrafanaRuleListItem (line 40) builds `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`)` with no returnTo. Users who click a rule in the filtered list and then try to go back lose their filter/search context. If this was intentional it should be noted; otherwise restore the returnTo parameter.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting() defeats the $__range guard and splits range-variable queries incorrectly

runSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on each target (line 299) before the queries are partitioned by querySupportsSplitting() (line 300). That function excludes queries containing $__range/$__range_ms/$_interval etc. via isQueryWithRangeVariable() precisely so they are NOT time-split (see the comment at lines 285-288: these variables are meant to be resolved by the backend against each sub-request's split time range). applyTemplateVariables runs templateSrv.replace with request.scopedVars, and panel/Explore requests include built-ins like __range in scopedVars, so a query such as count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) is rewritten to a fixed full-range duration (e.g. [2d]) before the guard runs. The guard then no longer matches, the query is classified as splittable and split into 1-day chunks, each of which evaluates a 2-day window: the chunks overlap, data is double-counted, and the combined result is wrong. Before this change these queries were sent as a single unsplit request. Either the range-variable check must run on the pre-interpolation expr, or interpolation must preserve/skip the built-in range variables.

Shard-split queries are template-interpolated twice

runShardSplitQuery() now applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables() to every target (line 52), and those interpolated targets are later passed as subRequest.targets into runSplitQuery() (line 163), which - after this same PR - applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again on each of them (querySplitting.ts line 299). The result is that every shard-split query is interpolated twice. Double interpolation is not idempotent: a literal escaped dollar written as $$var becomes $var after the first pass and is then expanded to the variable's value by the second pass, and variable values that themselves contain $ or text matching another variable name get re-expanded. Previously interpolation happened exactly once (via interpolateVariablesInQueries in runShardSplitQuery, with runSplitQuery doing none). The updated tests don't catch this because the mocked applyTemplateVariables only does a no-op-on-second-pass string replace. runShardSplitQuery should either skip its own interpolation now that runSplitQuery interpolates, or runSplitQuery needs a way to know the targets are already interpolated.

No regression test that $__range queries are still excluded from splitting after interpolation

The only new test ('Interpolates queries before execution') covers $__auto/$step interpolation, but there is no test asserting that a query using $__range (or another range variable) is still routed to the non-splitting group now that interpolation happens before the querySupportsSplitting()/isQueryWithRangeVariable() check in runSplitQuery. Since that guard inspects the raw expr for the literal $__range token and the new interpolation step can remove that token, a test pinning the 'queries with $__range are not split' behavior is needed to catch the regression; without it, the wrong-results scenario for range-variable queries ships silently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, performing the insert as two separate statements with no transaction or locking. Concurrent requests from different new devices (or requests hitting different Grafana instances behind a load balancer) can all read a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device limit by however many requests race in the window. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (it is now used to deny authentication), the count and insert need to be atomic, e.g. a single conditional upsert or a transaction with a locking read.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent requests can pass a non-atomic device count check and insert devices beyond the limit. Both recommend making the check and insert atomic using a transaction or locking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice treats 'row not updated' as 'device limit reached', locking out existing devices

When the limit is reached, updateDevice runs an UPDATE ... WHERE device_id = ? In both cases an existing device that should be allowed (or refreshed) is instead denied authentication with 'device limit reached'. The not-found condition should be distinguished from value-unchanged (e.g., use a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or check matched rows), and the stale-device case should be handled explicitly.

With the new device-limit feature, an unknown device beyond the limit makes CreateOrUpdateDevice return ErrDeviceLimitReached, so the request is rejected — but its cache entry has already been set. The very next request from the same device hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil without touching the database, TagDevice returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds. Consequence: an over-limit device (or an attacker generating new device IDs) gets anonymous access simply by retrying once, and the device is never recorded or counted. The cache entry must only be written after a successful store write (or removed on error). There is also no test covering the retry scenario, which would have caught this.

This adds database latency to anonymous page loads and makes anonymous auth fail whenever the device store is slow or unavailable (previously a store outage only logged a warning). The panic recovery that protected the request handler was also removed, so a panic inside TagDevice now propagates into the request. Only the limit-exceeded case needs to be synchronous; the common path (limit not reached or no limit configured) could remain asynchronous.

However I18n.translate in the accelerator only calls load_locale(config.locale), so the fallback locales' translation files stay unloaded unless someone explicitly called I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Background jobs (Sidekiq), ActionMailer deliveries, rake tasks and console code set I18n.locale directly without ensure_loaded!, so a lookup for a key missing in e.g. :fr will probe :en (or the default locale) while its YAML files are not loaded and will return 'translation missing: fr.xxx' even though the English translation exists. If an admin changes default_locale at runtime, translations previously resolved through the old default locale remain cached in the process-local LRU cache (size 300, so hot keys persist indefinitely) and users keep seeing the old language until eviction or restart. Nothing invalidates @cache when default_locale changes. The default locale (or a fallback-chain fingerprint) needs to be part of the cache key, or the cache must be flushed when the setting changes.

The 'is able to remove a member' test uses :delete correctly, so only the automatic-group guard test is testing the wrong verb.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same HTTP verb mismatch: the remove_member test calls xhr :put, while the route requires DELETE. The candidate's additional routing explanation does not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages off-by-one creates a phantom empty page

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 100 members with limit 50, i.e. exactly 2 pages), this yields 3, so showingLast (currentPage == totalPages) is never true on the real last page. The 'next' arrow stays enabled, and clicking it sets offset to min(offset+limit, user_count) = 100, which returns an empty member list while the pager shows '3/3'. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same off-by-one bug in Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1: exact multiples of the limit produce an extra page and allow navigation to an empty result page.

true_positives.golden_comment: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined
true_positives.matched_candidate:
findMembers returns undefined instead of a promise when name is empty

The guard clause changed from `return Ember.RSVP.resolve([])` to a bare `return;`. The method's contract was 'returns a promise'; the two current call sites happen not to chain on the result, but any caller doing `group.findMembers().then(...)` (as the previous versions of both routes did via afterModel, and as any plugin or future code would naturally write) will now throw TypeError on undefined. Keep returning a resolved promise for the empty-name case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify inconsistent return values: a code path returns undefined rather than the expected value. The candidate specifically identifies the empty-name guard's bare return and its impact on the promise-returning contract.

false_positives.candidate:
PUT /admin/groups/:id silently flips visible to false for old clients

The update action now reads flat params (params[:visible], params[:name], params[:alias_level]) instead of the previous nested params[:group][...] payload, and create likewise changed from params[:group][:name] to params[:name]. Any existing client (admin API script, plugin, or older cached frontend assets still in a user's browser) that PUTs group: {visible: "true", name: ...} will now hit `params[:visible] == "true"` evaluating to false, silently turning group visibility off, while the name and alias_level changes are silently dropped. The parameter format change breaks the published admin API contract with a data-corrupting failure mode rather than a loud error.

Unvalidated limit/offset in public members endpoint

The members action takes `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` and `offset = params[:offset].to_i` straight from the query string with no upper bound or sign check. The old code capped automatic-group listings at 200; now a single request with limit=100000000 forces the server to load and serialize the entire membership of a group (e.g. trust_level_0 can be every user on the site), an easy amplification/DoS vector on a public, non-admin endpoint. Additionally, negative values (limit=-1 or offset=-1) are passed to ActiveRecord's limit/offset and raise an unhandled error, returning a 500. Clamp limit (e.g. to a few hundred) and reject non-negative offset/limit.

Response shape of /groups/:name/members.json changed from array to object

The members endpoint previously rendered a bare JSON array of serialized members (`render_serialized(members.to_a, GroupUserSerializer)`) and now returns `{members: [...], meta: {total, limit, offset}}`. This is a public, user-facing endpoint; any consumer other than the in-repo frontend (themes, plugins, external API users parsing the array) will break, since code expecting an array will now iterate the object or read undefined. Even if intentional, this is an unversioned breaking change to a public API that should be called out and, ideally, covered by a controller spec — there are no tests at all for the new pagination/meta format.

Stale offset after removing a member leaves admin on an empty page

After removeMember succeeds it calls findMembers() with the old offset. The clamp on line 23 uses the client's stale user_count (still pre-removal), so e.g. with 51 members at offset 50, removing the last member re-requests offset 50; the server returns total=50, offset=50 and an empty members array. The UI then shows an empty member list with currentPage=2 and totalPages=1 (so showingLast is false and 'next' keeps firing no-op requests at the same offset). The offset should be re-clamped against the refreshed total (or reset toward the last valid page) when the response comes back.

save() error handler crashes when the rejection has no JSON body

The failure path does `$.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors` unconditionally. If the promise rejects for anything other than a JSON error response (network failure, timeout, gateway 502 returning HTML, or a rejection value without responseText), `e.responseText` is undefined, $.parseJSON throws, and the user gets no feedback at all (plus a JS error) instead of an alert. It also assumes the payload has an `.errors` key. Guard the parse and fall back to a generic message.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs database writes during model validation

BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator#validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation chain. Validation must be side-effect free: UsersController#create calls user.valid? (line 168) and then user.save, so every signup attempt runs validation twice and match_count/last_match_at are incremented twice per attempt. Any other code path that calls valid? on a User (e.g. User#change_username calls valid?) also performs an unexpected UPDATE on the blocked_emails table during what should be a read-only check. The collected statistics are therefore inflated and unreliable, and writes occur at times no caller expects them. Move the counter update out of the query path (e.g. record the hit only when a signup is actually rejected, or use a separate logging step).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: a blocking-check method unexpectedly writes statistics to the database during a read-like operation. The candidate adds validation-specific consequences, but these stem from the same side effects highlighted by the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass

should_block? looks up BlockedEmail.where(email: email) with an exact string match. The rest of the codebase normalizes emails (Email.downcase is used in UsersController#change_email and User.find_by_username_or_email), but nothing downcases the value here, and User#email is stored as submitted. A blocked address like 'spammer@example.com' can be re-used by signing up with 'Spammer@Example.com' or 'SPAMMER@example.com', defeating the entire blocklist feature. The lookup (and ideally the stored value) should compare downcased emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, which allows blocked users to bypass the blocklist by changing the capitalization of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates under concurrency

should_block? does a read-modify-write: it loads the record, does record.match_count += 1 in Ruby, then record.save. Two concurrent requests for the same blocked email both read the same count and both write count+1, so one increment is silently lost. Since this counter is the mechanism for tracking how often a blocked email attempts to register, it will undercount. Use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now]).

Any server email error permanently marks the email invalid with a misleading message

After a failed createAccount, the controller adds the email to rejectedEmails whenever the server response contains errors.email. This includes errors that are not about validity, such as 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist/blacklist 'not allowed from that email provider' message. Once added, emailValidation shows the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid') reason for that address with no way to distinguish causes, so a returning user who already has an account is told their email is simply invalid. Only add to rejectedEmails when the error is actually a blocked/invalid-email error (e.g. have the server send a distinguishable error code), or surface the server's real error message in the validation reason.

No tests for the whitelist/blacklist logic moved into EmailValidator

The EmailValidator spec only exercises the BlockedEmail branch, and it stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely. The domain whitelist/blacklist logic (email_in_restriction_setting? and both setting branches) was moved verbatim from User#email_validator into this new class but has no direct tests here, and no integration test covers that creating a User with an email present in blocked_emails actually fails. There is also no test for the case-sensitivity behavior of the blocked lookup. The core behavior of this PR (blocked emails reject signups end-to-end) is untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
-ms-align-items is not a real CSS property

The `align-items()` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. No such property exists — the Microsoft-prefixed old-syntax property is `-ms-flex-align`, which the mixin already emits on the previous line. The `-ms-align-items` declaration is invalid and will be dropped by every browser; it also fails CSS linting and can mislead future readers into thinking it does something. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that -ms-align-items is not a valid Microsoft-prefixed CSS property and that the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

false_positives.candidate:
Making .small-action a flex container silently disables float: right on its button

The PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, but the rule later in the same block still styles its `button { background: transparent; border: 0; float: right; }` (line 309). Children of a flex container become flex items and the `float` property is ignored on them, so the button (e.g. the banner/small-action close button) is no longer pushed to the right edge of the row. It will now render immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text, leaving a gap on the right and misplacing the control. The button needs `margin-left: auto` (or the container needs `justify-content: space-between`) to restore right alignment, as was done for `.panel` in header.scss. The same applies to `.topic-avatar { float: left; }` (line 270), though there the flex row layout coincidentally produces a similar result.

.panel right-alignment relies on margin-left: auto, which IE10 flexbox does not honor

The new flexbox mixins explicitly target IE10 by emitting `display: -ms-flexbox` / `-ms-flex-align`, but the header's right-hand `.panel` is positioned purely via `margin-left: auto` (the old `float: right` was removed). IE10's flexbox implementation does not support auto margins for main-axis alignment (alignment there must be done with `-ms-flex-pack`), so on IE10 the search/hamburger/user panel will not be pushed to the right edge of the header and will instead sit directly next to the title. Since the whole point of the `-ms-` prefixes in the mixins is to support that browser, `.contents` needs an `-ms-flex-pack: end`-style fallback (or the panel needs a different mechanism) for the layout to hold there.

align-items() mixin omits the -moz-box-align counterpart that flexbox()/order() imply

`flexbox()` emits `display: -moz-box` and `order()` emits `-moz-box-ordinal-group`, so the mixin set explicitly claims to support old-Gecko flexbox; but `align-items()` has no `-moz-box-align` line. Any browser that ends up using the `-moz-box` code path (the only one it is given) will get a flex container with no vertical alignment, so `.d-header .contents`, `.small-action`, and the `.badge-wrapper.bullet` would be laid out with the old default (stretch/start) instead of centered/baseline as intended. Either add `-moz-box-align` for symmetry or drop the `-moz-box` / `-moz-box-ordinal-group` output, since the two halves of the vendor story currently contradict each other.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' and is therefore dead code

The guard is defined as `def include_website_name` but ActiveModel::Serializers only invokes include methods named `include_#{attribute}?` — every other guard in this file (include_email?, include_stats?, include_card_image_badge?, etc.) follows that convention. Because of the missing '?', this method is never called, so the intended condition (only serialize website_name when the website is present) never takes effect. When a user has no website, the JSON will still contain a `website_name: null` key, and any future restriction logic added to this guard would silently not run.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same primary bug: include_website_name lacks the required '?' suffix, preventing the serializer from invoking it for conditional inclusion. It does not mention the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the conditional inclusion issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses untrusted-attribute hiding for TL0 profiles

The serializer registers :website as an untrusted attribute (untrusted_attributes list, lines 105-111), so when a TL0 user's profile is restricted from anonymous viewers (scope.restrict_user_fields?), the raw :website value is omitted from the JSON. The new :website_name attribute, however, is only listed in the plain `attributes` call (line 43) and its guard `include_website_name` (line 153) only checks `website.present?`. As a result, for restricted TL0 profiles the website host plus path (e.g. 'example.com/private-page') is still serialized and rendered on the profile, leaking exactly the information the hide-profiles setting is meant to conceal. It also breaks the template: since :website is omitted, user.hbs renders `<a href="">` (empty href pointing at the current page) with the leaked website_name as the link text. website_name must be added to untrusted_attributes (or its include method must check restrict_user_fields?).

Untrusted-attributes spec not updated for the new website_name attribute

The test at line 11 asserts that a fixed list of untrusted attributes (bio_raw, bio_cooked, bio_excerpt, location, website, profile_background, card_background) is omitted for TL0 users viewed anonymously, but :website_name was not added to that list. Because of this gap the suite passes even though website_name leaks the website host/path for exactly the profiles the setting protects. The spec should assert `expect(json).not_to have_key(:website_name)` in that context, which would have caught the privacy regression introduced by this change.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
postMessage origin check uses substring matching instead of exact origin comparison

The resize handler accepts messages when `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` is false, i.e. when the message origin appears anywhere as a substring of discourseUrl. That is not an equality check: any origin that happens to occur inside the discourseUrl string (e.g. as part of a path, or a shorter scheme/host prefix in some configurations) is accepted, and e.data.height is used unvalidated. The consequence is limited to resizing the iframe, but the check should compare `e.origin` against the exact expected origin (e.g. the parsed origin of discourseUrl) and the height coerced to a positive integer.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same origin-validation flaw: using indexOf substring matching instead of an exact origin comparison allows unintended origins to pass the check. The differing bypass examples and additional height-validation concern do not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Stored XSS: embed URL interpolated unescaped into raw HTML footer TopicEmbed.import builds the "Imported from" footer with `"#{url}"` — the URL is interpolated into HTML with no escaping, and the resulting post is stored with cook_method raw_html (cooked = raw, bypassing the sanitizing Markdown pipeline) and rendered in app/views/embed/best.html.erb with `raw post.cooked`. The only validation is `url =~ /^https?:///`, which permits quotes, `>`, and attribute-breaking characters. An attacker can hit /embed/best with a crafted embed_url whose host matches embeddable_host (e.g. `http:///?'>
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability in TopicEmbed.import caused by unescaped URL interpolation in generated HTML. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError, but directly matches the golden comment's XSS concern.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view can never render

The ERb at line 6 reads `<%- end if %>` with no condition following the `if` modifier. When ERb compiles the template the generated Ruby ends with `end if`, which is a syntax error (unexpected end-of-input). Any request to /embed/best for which a TopicEmbed exists (the main success path of this feature) will raise ActionView::Template::Error instead of rendering the comments. The controller specs never render views (TopicView is mocked, no render_views), so CI does not catch this — a view-rendering test is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same invalid ERB closing statement, `end if`, which causes a Ruby syntax error when rendering. The block should close with `end` alone.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil or failing feed item aborts the entire feed import with no per-item error handling

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every RSS/Atom item has content; for plain RSS 2.0 feeds without content:encoded, simple-rss returns nil for `i.content`, so this line raises NoMethodError on the first such item and the whole poll is aborted. Similarly, any exception raised while importing one item (bad URL, PostCreator failure — note that if the post fails to save, TopicEmbed.import still calls TopicEmbed.create! with a nil topic_id, raising RecordInvalid inside the transaction) prevents all subsequent items from being imported. Each item should be processed with its own error handling (and nil content handled, e.g. falling back to i.description).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that i.content can be nil in RSS feeds, causing i.content.scrub to raise an exception, and recommends falling back to i.description. This matches the golden issue, despite additional discussion of per-item error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated into a JS string literal without escape_javascript

The layout does `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')`. The referer is only validated to have a host equal to embeddable_host; its path/query can contain arbitrary characters (an attacker can send a request with a crafted Referer header directly — no control of a page on the host is needed). The value is placed in a single-quoted JavaScript string with no `j`/escape_javascript; it currently survives only because Rails' HTML escaping converts quotes to `'`, which then appears literally inside the script block, producing an invalid targetOrigin that makes postMessage throw a SyntaxError and breaks iframe resizing for such referers. It should be escaped with escape_javascript (and ideally the exact origin, not the full referer, used as targetOrigin).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify request.referer being interpolated into a JavaScript string without proper JavaScript escaping. Although the candidate emphasizes postMessage failures rather than XSS, it points to the same unsafe interpolation and missing escaping.

false_positives.candidate:
RSS item content imported as raw_html with no sanitization — stored XSS from feed content

poll_feed passes `i.content` (the raw HTML from the feed's content:encoded/body) straight into TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Post#cook then returns the raw string untouched, skipping the normal cooking/sanitizing pipeline, and best.html.erb renders it with `raw post.cooked`. Anyone who can influence the feed's HTML (compromised or malicious feed source at the admin-configured feed_polling_url) gets arbitrary JavaScript executed on the Discourse origin for every viewer, including logged-in staff. The readability path at least whitelists tags/attributes; the feed path has no equivalent. The imported HTML should be run through a sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist) before being stored as raw_html.

absolutize_urls raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs that pass the http(s) regex

TopicEmbed.import only gates on `url =~ /^https?:///`, but absolutize_urls then calls `URI(url)` which raises URI::InvalidURIError for URLs containing spaces or other invalid characters (e.g. `http://exa mple.com/post` or an unencoded `%zz`). Unlike TopicRetriever#invalid_host?, there is no rescue here, so a single malformed feed link (or a crafted embed_url) raises an unhandled exception. In PollFeed this aborts the remaining feed items; in RetrieveTopic the job fails. The URI parse should be guarded or the URL rejected up front with a full URI parse.

Feed and page fetches use open() with no timeout; a slow source hangs the job and the hourly schedule

`open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` (and `open(url)` in TopicEmbed.import_remote) use Kernel#open with no read/open timeout. The scheduled job has `retry: false` and is also invoked synchronously from TopicRetriever#perform_retrieve on a user-triggered retrieve, so a hanging or very slow feed server blocks a Sidekiq worker indefinitely and stalls subsequent scheduled runs. open-uri should be given `open_timeout`/`read_timeout` (or a job-level timeout).

setnx/expire are not atomic; a crash between them permanently disables retrieval for a URL

retrieved_recently? performs `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies between the two calls (or the expire fails), the key exists with no TTL and the URL is considered 'recently retrieved' forever — the embed will never be fetched again through the throttled path, leaving the loading page reloading every 30 seconds indefinitely. A single SET key 1 EX 60 NX (or a Lua script) should be used instead.

embed_url column is varchar(255); real URLs (plus the appended footer) can exceed it

The embed_url column is a Rails `string`, i.e. varchar(255) on PostgreSQL, with a NOT NULL constraint. Web page URLs frequently exceed 255 characters, and TopicEmbed.import additionally embeds the URL twice (href and text) into the post body; an over-long feed link will make the INSERT fail with 'value too long for type character varying(255)', aborting the import. The column should be text (or a larger limit) to match how URLs are stored elsewhere.

`force: true` added to an existing migration will drop an already-created top_topics table

This PR changes the previously shipped CreateTopTopics migration to `create_table :top_topics, force: true`. With force: true, create_table drops the table if it already exists; any environment that already ran the original migration and then re-runs it (db:migrate:redo, rebuilding from migrations rather than schema.rb) will silently lose all top_topics data. If the change was needed for test databases, it should be made in a separate migration or the test schema rebuilt, not by editing a released migration.

Only Gemfile_rails4.lock was updated; the default (Rails 3) lockfile is missing the new gems

The PR adds ruby-readability and simple-rss to the Gemfile and updates Gemfile_rails4.lock, but the repository's dual-boot setup (see the Bundler monkey patch at the top of the Gemfile) uses the default Gemfile.lock when booting in Rails 3 mode (`RAILS3` set), which per the diff was not regenerated. Any Rails 3-mode CI run or deployment will fail to resolve the new dependencies (TopicEmbed/poll_feed require them at runtime), so the Rails 3 lockfile needs the corresponding entries.

postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently overrides the width/height variant

In Ruby the second definition completely replaces the first, so the width/height variant is dead code. Any existing caller that invokes `downsize(from, to, width, height)` will now have its `height` argument bound to the `opts` parameter; when `optimize` evaluates `opts[:allow_animation]` on an Integer it raises `TypeError (no implicit conversion of Integer into Hash-like)`. Either remove the old signature entirely or rename/merge the two methods so the four-argument form still works.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB limit ignores admin-configured max upload sizes

validateUploadedFile now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024` KB instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, and the 413 handler at line 246 similarly hardcodes 10 MB instead of `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb`. This silently disables the `max_image_size_kb` and `max_attachment_size_kb` site settings on the client: admins who set a lower limit will see users attempting uploads up to 10 MB (which then fail server-side with a confusing error for attachments), and admins who set a higher limit will get an incorrect 'file too large' rejection in the browser. This looks like leftover debug/test code (the PR description is 'Test 1') and should be reverted to read the settings.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same hardcoded 10 MB upload limit replacing per-type site settings, causing client-side limits to diverge from configured server limits. It also explicitly covers the 413 handler.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop can never bring very large images under the limit and ignores downsize failures

The retry loop runs at most 5 iterations, each downsizing to '80%', so the best possible reduction is to 0.8^5 ≈ 33% of the original size. An image more than ~3x `max_image_size_kb` will still exceed the limit when the loop exits, and the oversized file is then passed to `Upload.create_for`, which will reject it — the user waits through 5 ImageMagim/ImageOptim passes only to get the same failure the feature was supposed to prevent. Additionally, the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize` is never checked: if conversion fails (e.g. unsupported/corrupt image or ImageMagick policy limits), the loop blindly retries five times and may hand a truncated/corrupted tempfile to `Upload.create_for`. The loop should either compute the exact target percentage needed in one pass or check the downsize result and bail out with a clear error.

allow_animation option never applies to uploads because animated-GIF detection relies on the file extension

The controller passes `allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` to `OptimizedImage.downsize`, but `OptimizedImage.optimize` (optimized_image.rb line 155) only chooses the animated code path when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`. The `from` path here is an uploaded/action-dispatched tempfile (RackMultipart-* or discourse-upload-*), which never ends in `.gif`, so animated GIFs are always processed through `convert #{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame. Even on sites with `allow_animated_thumbnails` enabled, every oversized animated GIF upload is silently stripped down to a single static frame — permanent loss of the original animation since the tempfile is downsized in place.

Hardcoded 10MB download cap regresses API uploads for sites with larger configured limits

The API URL-download path changed `FileHelper.download(url, SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes, ...)` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. On sites where an admin has raised `max_image_size_kb` above 10240 KB, remote images larger than 10 MB can no longer be fetched via the API at all (the download silently returns nil due to `rescue nil`, leading to a confusing failure downstream), even though such uploads were previously allowed. The cap should be derived from the setting (e.g. `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` plus some headroom to allow downsizing), not hardcoded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

The action should create/normalize the record via `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: ...)` like `set_notifications` does, which also correctly sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` and publishes the MessageBus `notification_level_change` event that the direct `tu.save!` path skips.

A logged-in user's browser can be made to hit this URL cross-site (e.g. an `` on an attacker page sends session cookies), silently muting or un-muting topics for the victim. Additionally, because the handler *toggles* state (watching/tracking -> regular, otherwise -> muted), any repeated visit — a page refresh, browser pre-render/prefetch of the email link, or a scanner following links in an open session — flips the user's notification level again, potentially re-subscribing someone who just unsubscribed. The builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. fall back to the preferences URL) or omit that sentence when it is absent, and this requirement needs a test.

Given the reachable nil crash and the CSRF-prone GET noted above, this endpoint needs specs covering: user with no TopicUser record, watching vs regular vs muted starting levels, wrong-slug redirect, and inaccessible topic.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

The script uses `sed -i '' -E "s|...|...|"` which is BSD/macOS syntax. On GNU sed (standard on Linux CI/dev containers), the empty-string argument after `-i` is not treated as an in-place suffix, so sed interprets `''` as the script and the substitution expression as a filename, causing the command to fail with an error and leaving `.env` unmodified (or worse, running the wrong edit). Use a portable approach (e.g. `sed -i.bak` + remove the backup, or detect the OS), since this script is committed to the shared repo.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same portability bug: the BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` syntax fails with GNU sed on Linux.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

deleteCache mutation never invalidates the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status in the UI

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check computes `end` identical to `start`, so slot end time is never validated

In the new working-hours check inside `checkIfIsAvailable`: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — `end` is the same expression as `start`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` only ever compares the slot's *start* minute against the working-hours end. A slot that starts within working hours but ends after them passes the check. `end` should be derived from the slot end (e.g. `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute() + eventLength`, or better from `slotEndTime`), otherwise this availability validation is wrong for any event whose slot would overrun the host's working hours.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the slot end time is calculated from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, allowing slots that extend beyond working hours to pass validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs object identity comparison `===` is always false, killing the start==end override case

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created Dayjs object references, which are always distinct, so this condition never fires (it is dead code). The intent was to detect overrides where start equals end (Cal.com's representation for an unavailable period). Because the check is dead, a slot that starts exactly at such an override's start time fails all the other conditions (`slotEndTime` is not before the start, `slotStartTime` is not after the end), `find` returns undefined, `dateOverrideExist` is true, and the function returns `true` — marking the slot available when the user explicitly blocked it. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `.valueOf()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === compares distinct Dayjs object references rather than date values, so the condition is always false. Both recommend .isSame() to compare values.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override bypass the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In `checkIfIsAvailable`, when a slot falls on a day that has a date override, `dateOverrideExist` is set to true inside the `dateOverrides.find()` callback, and the callback returns undefined for slots that are *within* the override window. Control then hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` and the function returns immediately, before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom. Consequence: for any slot covered by a date override, the host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are never consulted, so a host with a date override who already has a conflicting booking (Cal booking or external calendar event) will still be shown as available and can be double-booked. The override check must not short-circuit the busy check.

Date-override day comparison is formatted in the server's local timezone, making results server-TZ dependent

The day-match uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is explicitly UTC (`.utc()`), but the left-hand side is a plain Dayjs formatted without `.utc()`/`.tz()`, so it renders in whatever timezone the Node process runs in. On a server whose TZ is not UTC (common in non-UTC deployments), the same override/slot pair can land on different formatted days, so the override either fails to match (override ignored, host shown available on an overridden day) or matches the wrong day. Additionally, only the override's *start* day is compared, so an override window that crosses midnight UTC is only applied to one of the two UTC days it spans. The shifted value should be formatted with `.utc()` to match the right-hand side.

`override.timeZone` is used without a fallback although the type declares it optional

`const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();` assumes `override.timeZone` is always set, but this PR adds `timeZone?: string` to `TimeRange` as optional. Any caller of `getSlots` that supplies date overrides without a timezone (which the type explicitly permits — only the `getSchedule` call site populates it) will have dayjs fall back to the process/browser-local timezone for the offset computation, silently producing wrong override windows. Either make the field required on the `GetSlots` input type or fall back to `organizerTimeZone`.

The PR's primary bug fix (#8207) is that date overrides of *fixed* hosts are enforced for ROUND_ROBIN events (the new `isFixed`-aware filtering plus the date-override/working-hours logic in `checkIfIsAvailable`). The only test added exercises a single-user event's date override in a different invitee timezone; every team-event scenario in the suite uses `hosts: []` and no date overrides, so all round-robin hosts are loose hosts. There is no regression test where a fixed round-robin host has a date override and the slot list must be restricted accordingly — exactly the logic most likely to regress (and where the busy-check bypass above would be caught). Add a test with a ROUND_ROBIN event, one fixed host with a date override, one round-robin host without, asserting only the fixed host's override window is offered.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount incremented via read-modify-write instead of atomic increment

Both the failure branch (line 184) and the catch block (line 195) update retryCount with `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, using the value read at the start of the loop. If two cron invocations overlap, or the same reminder is processed concurrently, one increment is lost, so the reminder is retried more times than the intended two before deletion. Prisma supports an atomic form: `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`, which avoids the stale-read problem entirely.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same stale-read race in retryCount updates, which can lose increments under concurrent processing, and recommend Prisma's atomic increment in both the failure branch and catch block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

retryCount-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The deleteMany at the top of the handler now has an OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and no `scheduled: false`) filter, unlike the sibling branch. `retryCount` is a column on the shared WorkflowReminder model for all methods (EMAIL, SMS, WHATSAPP), so this SMS cron endpoint will delete any workflow reminder row of any method whose retryCount exceeds 1. Today only this endpoint writes retryCount, but the schema change makes the field available to every reminder type, and any other writer (e.g. a future WhatsApp/email retry mechanism, or manual data fixes) would have its rows silently destroyed by the SMS cron. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the retryCount > 1 deletion branch lacks a WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, allowing the SMS scheduler to delete non-SMS reminders. The candidate's additional scheduled:false suggestion does not change the underlying match.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders skipped for empty message or missing sendTo never increment retryCount and retry forever

The retry-count logic only runs inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When the message resolves to empty/null (e.g. no reminderBody and a non-REMINDER template) or `sendTo` is missing (e.g. the booking has no smsReminderNumber and the action is not SMS_NUMBER), neither the success nor the failure branch executes: the reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0 and is picked up again on every cron run until scheduledDate passes. This is exactly the endless-retry behavior the PR description says it is fixing, but for the 'silently skipped' class of failures. The else-branch (or an outer else) should also bump retryCount so these reminders are eventually cleaned up.

Failed reminders are hard-deleted, losing audit trail and referenceIds

Once a reminder exceeds the retry budget it is removed with `deleteMany`, which destroys the row including workflowStepId, bookingUid and any referenceId. There is no record that a reminder was attempted and abandoned, so neither support nor the booking owner can tell that an SMS reminder was dropped (e.g. due to an invalid phone number), and the failure reason is only available in server console logs. Consider marking the row (e.g. a status/needsAction flag) or logging the deleted reminder ids before removal, rather than silently deleting.

No tests for the new retry-count and deletion behavior

The PR adds a new state machine (retryCount incremented on Twilio failure or thrown error, rows deleted when retryCount > 1, deletion query rewritten as an OR) but ships no unit or integration tests. Worth covering at minimum: (1) a reminder whose scheduleSMS throws twice is deleted on the following run, (2) a reminder that succeeds after one failure is not deleted, (3) the deleteMany does not remove EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminders, and (4) reminders skipped due to missing sendTo do not loop forever.

This PR removes the public `findMany(findManyArgs)` method from InsightsBookingService and changes the return type of `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` from `Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput` to `Prisma.Sql`. No callers are updated anywhere in this PR, so any production code that calls `service.findMany(...)` or passes these conditions into a Prisma `where` clause (e.g. `where: { AND: [conditions] }`) will break - either a compile error or a runtime query-validation error. Note that the PR description claims only tests were updated because the service "was previously converted", but the diff shows the service conversion, including this API removal, happens in this PR. Assertions compare reduce-composed nested Prisma.Sql against flat template literals, and the tests were never executed

The PR author explicitly states the test runner failed, so none of these rewritten assertions have been verified. Several of them (team scope at line 296, org scope at line 333, combined filters at line 430) compare a condition the service builds by nesting `Prisma.Sql` objects (e.g. `Prisma.sql\`(${a}) OR (${b})\``, where `.values` contains `[Sql, Sql]` and `.strings` is `['(', ') OR (', ')']`) against a single flat template literal whose `.strings`/`.values` contain the raw scalars. `toEqual` performs deep structural comparison of the `Sql` objects, so unless Prisma flattens nested `Sql` at construction time, these assertions will fail even though the generated SQL is semantically identical. The org-scope assertion expects the `= ANY(...)` parameter arrays in a specific order ([org.id, team.id, team2.id, team3.id] and [user.id, user2.id, user3.id]), but the service builds these arrays from `TeamRepository.findAllByParentId` and `MembershipRepository.findAllByTeamIds`, which run `findMany` queries without an `orderBy` clause, so the database row order is not guaranteed. Since the new assertions deep-compare the `Prisma.sql` values arrays element-by-element, any different row ordering from Postgres makes the test fail intermittently even though `= ANY` is order-insensitive. Sort the expected IDs (or normalize both sides to sets) in the assertion to make the test deterministic.

This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

When the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token`, the code unconditionally sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This is not limited to the sync-enabled path — it also runs for the normal per-app schema. Microsoft's refresh-token endpoint legitimately omits `refresh_token` on refresh responses (the existing refresh token stays valid); previously Office365CalendarService preserved the old token via `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, but now the placeholder string "refresh_token" is spread over the real token and written to the DB. The candidate adds contextual details without changing the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no custom toString), so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown-optional }`. The comment claims "any property with a number is the expiry" but nothing like that is implemented — no expiry field is validated. Callers that persist this data — Google CalendarService (`data: { key }`) and Salesforce (`data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, ... } }`) — will save credentials that have lost `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, `instance_url`, `scope`, etc., permanently corrupting the stored credential. true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget; handler returns before cancellation is persisted

In handleCancelBooking.ts (lines 485-493) `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async functions invoked inside a `forEach` without being awaited, and the request responds immediately afterwards. All of the new cancellation logic (marking the WorkflowReminder row `cancelled: true`, deleting unscheduled rows, calling SendGrid/Twilio) therefore runs after the response has been sent. On serverless platforms (cal.com runs on Vercel) background work after the response is not guaranteed to complete; if the function is frozen or recycled the reminders are never marked cancelled and the emails/SMS are still sent for the cancelled booking — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The same unawaited pattern exists in packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx lines 488-494 (requestReschedule) and packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts lines 966-972 (reschedule path, which is even wrapped in a try/catch that can never catch anything because the promises are never awaited). These calls should be collected and awaited before returning.

Although it does not mention workflow or workflow-step updates/deletions, it directly matches the cause and consequence described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

immediateDelete branch leaves no persistent state and no retry on failure

When `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called with `immediateDelete: true` and a `referenceId`, it POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns without deleting the row or setting `cancelled: true`. If the SendGrid request fails (e.g. the 100-pending-cancellations limit this PR describes, a network error, or an already-processed batch), the error is swallowed by the catch and the reminder row is left with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled` unset — so the cron-based retry mechanism will never pick it up and the email is still sent. For comparison, the non-immediate path at least persists `cancelled: true` so the cron retries. The immediate path should also mark the row (e.g. set `cancelled: true` before the request, or keep the row on failure) so a failed cancellation is recoverable. This path is used by the reschedule flow in handleNewBooking.ts, so a failed cancel here means the attendee gets a reminder for the old booking time.
