The candidate emphasizes failed-cancellation recovery and does not mention the omitted SendGrid DELETE call, but it identifies the same core database-state bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellations within the last cron interval before the send date are still too late

Booking cancellation only sets `cancelled: true` on the WorkflowReminder; the actual SendGrid cancellation happens in this cron job, but only for reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour, and the cron runs every 15 minutes. If a booking is cancelled when its reminder's `scheduledDate` is less than one cron interval away, the next cron run happens after the email has already been sent. Worse, the `deleteMany` at the top of the handler (lines 34-41) deletes all EMAIL reminders with `scheduledDate <= now` — including ones marked `cancelled: true` that were never cancelled at SendGrid — so the missed cancellation is silently cleaned up with no retry and no error. Consider using the `immediateDelete` path (already implemented and used for reschedules) for reminders whose `scheduledDate` is imminent, or at minimum cancelling reminders whose date has just passed instead of deleting them.

One failed SendGrid cancellation aborts all remaining cancellations in the cron run

In the cancellation loop (lines 53-77) each `client.request` cancel call is awaited inside a single try/catch that wraps the whole loop, and the prisma deletes are only executed after the loop completes. If any single cancel request throws (invalid batch id, rate limit, already-processed batch — e.g. batches created for EMAIL_ADDRESS steps where no message was ever sent), the exception jumps straight to the catch: none of the remaining reminders in `remindersToCancel` are cancelled at SendGrid, and none of the DB deletes run. Since all of these reminders have `scheduledDate` within the next hour, they will be sent even though their bookings were cancelled. Each cancel/delete should be handled in its own try/catch so one bad batch id cannot block the rest.

Race: booking cancelled while cron is scheduling its reminder still results in the email being sent

The cron fetches all unscheduled reminders at line 80 and then iterates them, calling `sgMail.send` (line 196) before updating the row with the batch id (line 211). If a booking is cancelled while this loop is running (the loop performs multiple awaits per reminder and can easily run for minutes with many reminders), the cancel path deletes the reminder row (the `!referenceId` branch of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`), but the cron has already read the row into memory and still sends the email. The subsequent `prisma.workflowReminder.update` fails with P2025, which is only caught and logged, and the batch reference is never stored, so the sent email cannot be cancelled afterwards. The handler should re-check that the reminder still exists and is not `cancelled` immediately before calling `sgMail.send`, or perform the row update (e.g. claim it) before sending.

No tests for the new reminder cancellation logic

This PR changes the core cancellation contract (new `cancelled` flag, deferred cron-based SendGrid cancellation, three distinct branches in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, immediate vs. deferred delete semantics across five call sites) but adds no unit or integration tests anywhere in the PR. The behavior has several boundary conditions that regress easily (reminder with null referenceId, immediateDelete flag, cancellation window in the cron, reschedule path). At minimum the branching of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and the cron's cancel-selection query (`cancelled: true` AND `scheduledDate` within 1 hour) should be covered by tests.

EventManager is built with the requesting user's credentials, not the booking organizer's

The handler authorizes team admins/owners and attendees (not just the organizer) to add guests, but then constructs `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })` using `ctx.user` (the caller) and credentials from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`. When a team owner or an attendee triggers this mutation, the calendar update (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`) runs with the wrong user's calendar credentials — most likely none matching the booking's destination calendar — so the external calendar event is not updated for the new guests, or the operation errors. The EventManager should be constructed from the booking organizer (`booking.user`, which is already included with credentials in the initial query) so calendar attendee updates work regardless of who calls the endpoint.

The handler never checks `booking.status`, so guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings; those guests then receive an email with an ICS of `status: "CONFIRMED"` (attendee-add-guests-email.ts line 15) for an event that no longer exists. Additionally, for event types with `seatsPerTimeSlot`, the handler blindly `createMany`s attendees with no capacity check and without creating the associated `seatsReferences`/booking-seat records that the seats flow relies on, which can overbook a seat-limited event and leave attendee records in a state that breaks seat cancellation logic.

The catch block is `catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }` — the caught `err` is discarded, no logger is used, and the mutation still returns success ("Guests added"). Additionally, `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), "error")` never falls back because a template literal is always truthy, so the newly added "unable_to_add_guests" locale string is dead code. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code single-use enforcement is not atomic (read-modify-write race)

In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup-code check does a read of the decrypted backupCodes array, an indexOf lookup, and then a separate prisma.user.update that writes back the whole array. Two concurrent sign-in requests using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so one single-use code authenticates twice; likewise two concurrent logins with different codes will each write their own copy of the array and the last write wins, resurrecting a code the other request already consumed. The code is also consumed (nulled and persisted) before next-auth finishes creating the session, so any later failure (JWT encode error, network drop mid-request) burns the code without a successful login. Single-use consumption should be made atomic/transactional and only committed once authentication has succeeded.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both pass validation before either update is persisted, allowing a one-time code to authenticate more than once. Its additional concerns do not negate this direct match.

onEnable is only invoked via the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog any other way leaves the 2FA switch out of sync

If the user closes the dialog via ESC, the dialog's built-in close affordance, or onOpenChange (all wired directly to the onOpenChange prop), neither onEnable nor onCancel fires and the modal state is not reset. The security settings page will continue to show 2FA as disabled even though it is actually enabled in the database, and the dialog's internal step state persists for the next open. The accompanying message ("No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." in common.json) is misleading because there is no settings flow that generates codes while 2FA is enabled — the only path is to disable 2FA (using the TOTP they may have lost) and re-enable it. Either a regeneration endpoint is needed or the message must tell the user their actual recovery option.

The e2e changes only exercise the backup-codes display step (download filename, copy toast, close button). The show/hide password toggle button in PasswordField now has tabIndex={-1}, making it unreachable by keyboard in every password field across the app (login, 2FA setup/disable, etc.). Keyboard-only users can no longer verify what they typed into a password field. If the goal was to stop Enter on the toggle from submitting the surrounding form, the button already has type="button"; excluding it from tab order is an accessibility regression rather than a fix.

Per-process SpansBuffer memory info double-counts Redis clusters, skewing the hard-backpressure ratio

In `submit()` (lines 297-304) the code now aggregates `get_memory_info()` across one SpansBuffer per flusher process. Each shard-group buffer returns memory stats for every Redis cluster its shards live on, so a cluster that hosts shards in several process groups is counted once per group. The `used / available` ratio is then weighted by how the shards happen to be distributed across processes rather than by actual cluster memory: a nearly-full cluster whose shards fall into only one process group can be diluted below `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` by other, emptier clusters, delaying the 'Pausing consumer due to Redis being full' backpressure until Redis actually evicts data. Adding `String getShortcut();` as an abstract method to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a source- and binary-incompatible change: every existing custom grant-type factory deployed as an extension will fail to compile against the new version, and pre-built jars will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when Keycloak's DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory calls getShortcut() during postInit (which happens at server startup, so the whole server can fail to boot for those deployments). Provide a `default` implementation (e.g. deriving a shortcut from getId() or returning a documented fallback) to preserve compatibility.

It was part of the public SPI surface (this class lives in server-spi-private and is implemented/used by third-party grant extensions), so removing it is a compile-time break for any external code that wrapped or derived a Context. (2) The new `grantType` field is captured once in the constructor from `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`, but `setFormParams(...)` (which external grant implementations can use to swap in re-parsed form params) does not refresh `grantType`. Consequently, when token issuance later reads `context.getGrantType()` in OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse and encodes it into the access-token ID, the encoded grant type can be wrong/stale relative to the form params actually in effect, silently corrupting the context metadata this PR introduces.

Lazy map refresh can silently corrupt grant-type/shortcut mappings on shortcut collisions

In getShortcutByGrantType (and getGrantTypeByShortcut), when a grant type is not found in the cached maps, the factory refreshes the cache by blindly doing `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` without checking whether that shortcut is already mapped to a different grant type. If a newly deployed custom grant reuses a shortcut already assigned to another grant (e.g. "ac"), the put overwrites the existing reverse mapping, and from then on tokens containing that shortcut decode to the wrong grant type — data corruption in the token context with no warning. Note the duplicate-shortcut validation only runs once in postInit (line 82), so dynamically deployed/hot-reloaded grants bypass it entirely. The lazy refresh path should detect the collision (existing mapping to a different grant) and fail loudly (log error / throw) instead of overwriting, mirroring the postInit validation.

getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext determines the token type via AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session), which evaluates `session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(USE_LIGHTWEIGHT_ACCESS_TOKEN_ENABLED)`. TokenManager.initToken receives the issuing `client` as a parameter, but this path relies on the ambient session-context client being set to the same client; where they diverge (or where the session-context client is null, e.g. token creation invoked from non-request contexts such as backchannel flows or tests), the lookup either returns the wrong client's lightweight setting or throws an NPE. When user.credentialManager().updateCredential() succeeds (user-storage path), createRecoveryCodesCredential() returns without touching the Keycloak DB. A federated user who already has a recovery-authn-codes credential in local storage (e.g. set up before the storage provider supported the type, or during a setup where the storage transiently returned false from updateCredential) keeps that old credential valid after regenerating codes: SubjectCredentialManager.isValid() validates local stored credentials for federated users as well, so previously generated (possibly compromised) codes remain usable, and RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()'s federated-first ordering means the login UI prompts based on the new credential while the old one still authenticates. It does not verify the properties that make recovery codes safe: (1) that a code already used for a login is rejected on a second attempt (which, given the current implementation, would fail - see the consumption gap for federated credentials), (2) that after re-running the required action the previously generated codes no longer authenticate, and (3) that once all codes are exhausted the user is prompted to set up new codes. However, the same PR modifies operator/scripts/Dockerfile-custom-image to run `kc.sh build ... --features=rolling-updates`, so the feature is enabled inside the image the tests deploy regardless of the CR. A real user deploying a stock image without the feature would hit the documented failure, which no test covers. Either the parameterization should explicitly enable/disable the feature in the CR for both strategies, or a negative test for the feature-disabled failure should be added.

The PR introduces exit code 4 (CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED) and documents it in docs/guides/server/update-compatibility.adoc as the contract for CI/CD scripts ("Exit Code 4: Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The feature `rolling-updates` is disabled."). The `metadata` subcommand (update-compatibility metadata) also exits with code 4 when the feature is disabled (UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()), but in that case no rolling-upgrade evaluation happened and no metadata was produced — it is simply a command failure. Script authors handling both subcommands with one exit-code table will misinterpret a code 4 from `metadata` as an incompatibility verdict rather than 'the command did not run'. The table should state that exit code 4 means the command was not executed because the feature is disabled.

With MgmtPermissionsV2.groups() now returning GroupPermissionsV2, deleting any group fires the event and the listener throws, failing the group deletion (and if only V2 is enabled the listener is not registered, so per-group resources/policies are never cleaned up and stale authorization data accumulates). These operations need real V2 implementations (e.g. resource/policy cleanup) rather than throwing.

In GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest, testManageAllGroups creates the group "testGroup" (later renamed to "newGroup") via ApiUtil.handleCreatedResponse without registering a realm.cleanup() entry (compare the other tests that do `realm.cleanup().add(r -> r.groups().group(id).remove())`), and testManageGroup creates "subGroup" through the subGroup(...) call at line 226 (expecting 201) also without cleanup. Depending on JUnit's method execution order, the leaked groups make these assertions fail intermittently.

Group resources fall through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which for per-group resources created by getOrCreateResource is the raw group ID (the resource name). Permission/resource listings in the admin API and console will therefore show bare UUIDs for group permissions instead of a group name or path, unlike users.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
order() added as an abstract method breaks the public CryptoProvider SPI

The new int order() method was added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation. CryptoProvider is an SPI intended to be implemented outside the Keycloak tree (the same repo has three implementations and third-party/forks exist, e.g. in the keycloak-client repo that this PR's description says will be synced later). Any existing compiled implementation of CryptoProvider will still load via ServiceLoader but will throw AbstractMethodError as soon as CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() calls order() on it during sorted(...), breaking initialization of those deployments at runtime, and source-level implementors fail to compile. Declaring it as default int order() { return 0; } would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing the authz-client provider (order 100) to lose against the built-in providers (order 200).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. order() was added as an abstract method to CryptoProvider without a default, which breaks backward compatibility for existing implementations.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; selection between equal-order providers is classpath-dependent and only logged at DEBUG

detectProvider() previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which was a deliberate fail-fast guard (e.g. against having both keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402 present). Now it silently picks the provider with the highest order(). All three in-tree providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return order() == 200, so when more than one of them is present the winner is decided by ServiceLoader encounter order, i.e. by classpath/JAR ordering, which is not deterministic across deployments. Concretely: a FIPS deployment that accidentally also has keycloak-crypto-default on the classpath can silently initialize and register the plain (non-FIPS) BouncyCastle provider instead of BCFIPS, with no error; the 'Ignored crypto providers' message is emitted only at DEBUG level so operators will not notice the wrong provider being used. Either give the providers distinct orders, break ties deterministically, or at least log the ignored providers at WARN.

Provider only implements ECDSA r/s conversion, but registers globally and is latched by AuthzClient.create() for the whole JVM

AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException for getAlgorithmProvider(), getPemUtils(), getKeyFactory(), getSignature(), getX509CertFactory(), createECParams(), etc. However it is registered through META-INF/services and AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...), which sets the JVM-wide static provider. keycloak-core code that authz-client users commonly exercise routes through these methods: org.keycloak.common.util.PemUtils' PEM key/certificate decoding goes through CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getPemUtils(), and JWS signing helpers go through getAlgorithmProvider()/getSignature(). Concretely, an application that uses only the authz-client artifact (the exact scenario this PR targets - no BouncyCastle-based provider on the classpath, so the order-100 stub wins) and configures signed-JWT client credentials (jwt client authenticator) will hit UnsupportedOperationException when decoding the PEM private key, a feature the authz-client supports. There is no test or analysis in the PR demonstrating that the implemented surface (only ECDSA r/s conversion) covers what the authz-client actually invokes through CryptoIntegration; at minimum the JWT client-credentials flow should be tested end-to-end with this provider as the only one on the classpath.

ECDSA test round-trip is too weak to catch truncation/padding bugs and misses leading-zero edge cases

The test only checks that concat -> DER -> concat is self-consistent (rsConcat == rsConcat2). It never asserts that the re-encoded DER equals the original minimal-DER signature produced by JCA (Arrays.equals(sign, asn1Des)), so a bug that truncates or mis-pads r/s on the concat side could still pass, since the same buggy conversion is applied in both directions. Additionally, each test signs once with a freshly generated key, so the probability of exercising the tricky edge cases - r or s whose encoding has a leading zero byte or is shorter than the curve length, which is exactly what the hand-rolled ASN.1Encoder/ASN1Decoder code must handle via integerToBytes and the len+1 zero-padding - is roughly 1/256 per component per run and effectively never happens. The test should loop over many signatures (or use fixed vectors with known leading-zero r/s values) and also assert DER equality against the original signature bytes.

No test for the new order-based provider selection logic

The core behavior change of this PR - CryptoIntegration now tolerates multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath and selects the one with the highest order() instead of throwing IllegalStateException - has no test coverage anywhere in the changed files. A regression in the comparator (e.g. dropping .reversed() would silently pick the lowest-order provider, meaning AuthzClientCryptoProvider would win over DefaultCryptoProvider in the testsuite) or in the tie-breaking would go unnoticed. A unit test should assert that with two providers of different order the higher one is selected, and document/assert the intended behavior for equal orders, since all three built-in providers currently return 200.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result intentionally slices the queryset with a negative start index when `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0` (line 880, `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`). The comment claims "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically," but this is false: Django raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for any queryset sliced with a negative index. Since the audit log endpoint feeds an `AuditLogEntry.objects.filter(...)` QuerySet into this paginator, any request with a negative-offset cursor will crash with a 500 error instead of returning results. The same problem exists in the `is_prev` branch shared with BasePaginator (line 184), where `start_offset = offset` is used unclamped for previous-page cursors, so a client-crafted cursor like `0:-5:1` also produces a negative slice and a 500.

The candidate's extra note about the is_prev branch is additional detail and does not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with datetime sort keys used by the audit log endpoint

The endpoint instantiates OptimizedCursorPaginator with `order_by="-datetime"`, but the paginator's `get_item_key` (line 838-840) does `int(math.floor(value))` on the raw attribute, which is a `datetime` for this model. `math.floor` on a datetime raises `TypeError`, and unlike DateTimePaginator there is no strftime/multiplier conversion to a numeric epoch value. `get_item_key` is invoked by `build_cursor`/`_build_next_values` on every result, so even if the TypeError from the `paginate()` call signature were fixed, every optimized-path request would crash when building the next/prev cursors. The cursor values produced are also semantically different from DateTimePaginator's (raw value vs. milliseconds-since-epoch), so cursors are not interchangeable between the two paginators.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue as the golden comment. get_item_key calls math.floor on a datetime value because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by=-datetime, and this raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
`enable_advanced_features` is not an accepted argument of `Endpoint.paginate`

The optimized branch calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`. Sentry's `Endpoint.paginate` (in sentry/api/base.py) has no `enable_advanced_features` parameter — extra paginator constructor arguments must be passed via the `paginator_kwargs` dict. Any request with `optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser or global-access member will raise `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'` and return a 500, so the entire new code path can never succeed.

Client-switchable paginator silently changes cursor semantics mid-pagination

The paginator used depends on the per-request `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter. A client that pages through audit logs with the default DateTimePaginator receives cursors whose `value` is a milliseconds-since-epoch number (DateTimePaginator.multiplier = 1000); if the same client then sends that cursor with `optimized_pagination=true`, OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw integer and compares it directly against the `datetime` column in `build_queryset` (line 857). This produces wrong result windows (duplicated or skipped rows) rather than an error, because the two paginators disagree on the meaning of the cursor value. Cursor interpretation should not depend on an unrelated query flag toggled per request.

The PR adds a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator), modifies the slicing logic in BasePaginator.get_result used by every cursor-paginated endpoint in the codebase, and adds a new request branch in the audit logs endpoint, but includes no tests. Basic coverage would have caught the crash-on-use defects (unsupported paginate kwarg, negative-offset slicing AssertionError, datetime key TypeError) and would guard the BasePaginator slicing change against regressions for existing consumers.

The added comment states "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / This enables efficient reverse pagination," but the code below it (`self.offset = int(offset)`) is unchanged from before — it already accepted any int. The comment documents a behavior that does not exist and contradicts the rest of the pagination stack, which will mislead future maintainers.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the entire function, which (coarsely) guaranteed that only one build per key could run at a time and that GetIndex would block rather than return nil mid-build. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. The caller, searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go:287), does a check-then-build with no per-key synchronization (its own TODO comment admits this: "We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key... simple mutex not great"). With the lock removed, two concurrent Search requests (or a Search request racing a watch-event-triggered build in handleEvent) for a namespace whose index doesn't exist yet will both see GetIndex return nil and both invoke BuildIndex for the same key. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory, which fails or corrupts the on-disk index; for in-memory indexes the build runs twice, IndexedKinds/IndexTenants metrics are double-counted, and the index object that loses the cache-map race is the one that handleEvent may keep writing watch events into, so those updates silently disappear from searches. A per-key singleflight/mutex is needed to preserve the exclusion the old lock provided.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same race. Narrowing b.cacheMu in BuildIndex to cover only the final cache assignment lets concurrent goroutines build the same index for the same key. The golden comment points to this exact cause and effect.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs reads b.cache without acquiring cacheMu

bleveBackend.TotalDocs iterates b.cache with no lock while BuildIndex mutates the map under cacheMu. TotalDocs is invoked at the end of searchSupport.init (search.go:216), which now overlaps with the just-started watch goroutine: handleEvent can trigger getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex -> cache write for a namespace not covered at startup, concurrently with the TotalDocs read. That is an unsynchronized map read/write and can panic (concurrent map iteration and map write). Take b.cacheMu.RLock in TotalDocs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while the watcher goroutine started just above can concurrently trigger a BuildIndex write to the map, which can panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Reordering Init so the watcher starts after index build silently drops all writes made during indexing

Init previously called s.initWatcher() before s.search.init(); it now runs the search index build first and only starts the event watcher afterwards. The SQL backend's WatchWriteEvents (pkg/storage/unified/sql/backend.go:558) initializes its poller's `since` watermark from the *current* latest resource versions at the moment it is called, so every write that occurs while the (potentially long) index build is running is never picked up: it is neither broadcast to Watch subscribers (the Broadcaster/mostRecentRV only see post-start events) nor reflected anywhere. Before this change the watcher was running during index construction, so those events were streamed to clients. The consequence is that any write landing in the startup-indexing window is silently lost from watch streams. The build path already computes the last-read resource version (comment in search.go:375: "when watching, we must add all events since that time"), but nothing uses it; the watcher should be started before or seeded from the index build's RV rather than from latest.

Data race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` in init's errgroup workers

In searchSupport.init, the errgroup closures assign to the captured outer variables `err` (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`, line 190) and increment `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) from multiple concurrent goroutines with no synchronization. This is a data race under the Go memory model. It was mostly latent before because bleveBackend.BuildIndex serialized workers behind its whole-function cacheMu lock, but this PR removes that lock specifically to let builds run concurrently, making the race real. Consequences range from torn counters in the "namespaces indexed" span attribute to one goroutine's error return value being overwritten/observed inconsistently by another. Capture local variables inside the closure and use an atomic counter for the total.

Failed Init in NewResourceServer leaks the context and partially started goroutines

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns `nil, err` on failure, but never calls s.cancel() on the error path. If any stage of Init fails partway (e.g., lifecycle hooks succeed, search init starts its event-consumer goroutine, then initWatcher fails), the server object is discarded while the cancelable context and any goroutines spawned during partial initialization keep running. Notably, the searchSupport watch goroutine (search.go:207-213) consumes from the events channel on a context.Background() with no shutdown path at all, so it polls and processes events forever for a server that was never returned to the caller. Call s.cancel() (and ideally give the search watch goroutine a stop mechanism) before returning the error.

Postgres path of the storage-server integration test is now skipped entirely

The test now skips unconditionally for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres ("test not working with postgres in Drone"), which means the storage server target and the addStorageServerToConfig postgres branch (db_host/db_name/db_user/db_pass keys, lines 75-79) get no CI coverage at all — that configuration code can silently rot. Since the PR also changes startup behavior of this exact target, losing the postgres coverage increases the risk of merging a startup regression undetected. Preferably fix the Drone environment issue; otherwise at least track it so the skip is temporary.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() permanently kills the factory-owned queue pool; any Kafka rebalance silently drops all subsequent messages

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and calls queue.shutdown() on every work queue. However, the queue_pool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and shared by every strategy the factory builds. Arroyo's StreamProcessor tears down the old strategy and calls create_with_partitions() again on every rebalance/partition reassignment, which is routine in production. After the first rebalance, the new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wraps a pool whose queues are shut down: FixedQueuePool.submit() -> work_queue.put() raises ValueError, which is swallowed by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (line 317), which marks the offset complete so it gets committed. The result is that after any rebalance, every message is silently dropped while offsets advance, i.e. total silent data loss. The pool's lifecycle must be owned by the factory (only shut down in factory.shutdown()), not by each strategy instance.

Failed messages are marked complete and committed, contradicting the documented 'only commits offsets after successful processing' guarantee

OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when self.result_processor(...) raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325) does the same when decoding or grouping_fn raises. The class docstring claims 'No item is lost' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing', but the implementation is at-most-once: a message whose handling fails is logged and its offset committed, so it is never retried or DLQ'd. This is a different failure semantic from other arroyo strategies (RunTask/BatchStep propagate errors so the processor can retry), so operators switching modes will silently lose data that used to be retried. Either the docstring/guarantees must be corrected or failures should keep the offset outstanding (or route to a DLQ).

Graceful shutdown does not drain queued items and the commit thread is stopped before draining, so shutdown loses in-flight work boundaries

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker's loop condition ('while not self.shutdown') is checked after each item, so a worker with a backlog exits after its current item, leaving the remaining queued items unprocessed even though q.shutdown(immediate=False) was specifically chosen to allow draining. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (line 335) stops and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining items, so offsets for items completed during the drain are never committed and those messages are re-consumed (and re-processed, possibly non-idempotently) after restart. The shutdown path should let workers drain the queues first (the queue.ShutDown from q.shutdown(immediate=False) already terminates them), and run a final commit pass after draining.

OffsetTracker stalls forever on permanent offset gaps and does an O(offset-range) scan every second

get_committable_offsets() breaks at the first offset not present in all_offsets and only ever commits up to that point, assuming any gap will eventually be filled by a message passed to submit(). But offsets can be permanently absent from the consumer's view - e.g. Kafka transactional control records that librdkafka filters out, or offsets skipped after consumer-group offset expiry - so a gap that never fills blocks all commits for that partition for the life of the process, causing unbounded offset lag and rebalance risk. Additionally, the scan iterates range(start, max_offset + 1) every second; with such a permanent gap the range grows unboundedly (min to max of ever-seen offsets), making each commit tick progressively more expensive. A safer design is to track only the set of outstanding offsets and commit min(outstanding)-1, rather than requiring contiguity.

Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure despite the documented claim

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately after put(), so the arroyo consumer thread keeps fetching and enqueueing messages as fast as Kafka delivers them. If workers fall behind (the exact 'one slow item clogs a queue' scenario the PR is meant to mitigate, now per-queue instead of per-batch), memory grows without bound and consumer lag accumulates invisibly. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The queues should be constructed with a bounded maxsize (queue.put then blocks the arroyo thread, applying real backpressure), or another bound on in-flight messages is needed.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling is racy and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation

The test asserts that no commit happens for a partition after a processing failure ('assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets'). But OrderedQueueWorker completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises, so once the 1-second commit tick fires the strategy will commit offset 102 for the partition. The test only passes if it finishes its wait/sleep before the commit thread's next tick, making it timing-dependent and flaky. It also masks the at-most-once data-loss behavior of the finally-block completion (see the worker implementation); either the implementation or the test's expectation needs to be fixed so they agree deterministically.

test_stats_reporting races on queue depth and test_different_groups_distributed can flake under hash randomization

In test_stats_reporting, 10 items are submitted to a pool whose workers are already running a trivially fast result_processor, and the test immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0; if the workers drain the queue before get_stats() is called, the assertion fails intermittently. Similarly, test_different_groups_distributed asserts all 3 queue indices are hit by 20 hashed group keys; since string hashes are randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), the mapping is effectively random each run and there is a small but real chance (~0.1%) that only 2 of 3 buckets are used, causing an intermittent failure. These assertions should be made deterministic (e.g., block the workers, or assert the index is within range rather than full coverage).

'offsets_committed' metric counts partitions, not offsets

In _commit_loop, the metric 'remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.offsets_committed' is incremented by len(committable), which is the number of partitions in the commit dict, not the number of Kafka offsets advanced. For a busy consumer committing thousands of offsets per tick across a few partitions, the metric dramatically undercounts and its name misleads anyone dashboarding it. It should report the sum of offset deltas (or be renamed to partitions_committed).

New `optimized_pagination` query-parameter code path is undocumented and completely untested

This PR adds a new, undocumented request parameter (`optimized_pagination=true`) that switches a public (albeit EXPERIMENTAL) endpoint to a different paginator and enables an 'advanced features' mode, gated on `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`. There are no tests for this path anywhere in the PR, no API documentation for the new parameter, and no explanation of what it actually optimizes (the paginator is functionally identical to the default except for a negative-offset branch that crashes — see other findings). The PR description is just 'Test 2', which suggests this change was not reviewed as a deliberate feature. Given the path is broken for its only configured sort key (datetime), the lack of tests is why that was not caught.

zunionstore merges use the default AGGREGATE SUM, corrupting scores of payloads present in both keys

Both merge operations (`redis.call("zunionstore", set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` at lines 47 and 53) omit an AGGREGATE argument, so Redis defaults to SUM. When the same span payload exists in both source keys — which happens under Kafka's at-least-once delivery, e.g. a span delivered in one batch lands in the set keyed by its parent while a duplicate delivery in a later batch lands in the merged set — the resulting member's score is the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values. Since the score is the span's end timestamp used to order the zset, this silently doubles the timestamp. The consequences are that zpopmin eviction (which pops the lowest scores) evicts the wrong spans, and the flush-time iteration order no longer reflects chronological order. The previous sunionstore-based code had no score semantics so this was not an issue; the fix is to pass `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) to both zunionstore calls.

New span eviction (zpopmin at 1000) silently drops span data with no metric or log, and can evict the segment's root span

The script now evicts the lowest-scored (oldest end_timestamp) members whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Unlike the previous behavior — where oversized segments were skipped at flush time with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log — this eviction is completely silent: there is no metric, no log, and no marker on the flushed segment, so the ongoing data loss is invisible to operators. Additionally, if the segment/root span is among the evicted members (possible whenever its end_timestamp is not the maximum, e.g. async traces), the segment is flushed without any root span, so no span gets `is_segment=True`, while the `span-buf:hrs:` key still reads "1" and forces the shorter root timeout. The limit is also hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, diverging from the Python-side `max_segment_spans` config (default 1001), which this PR leaves as a dead, unused parameter in SpansBuffer.__init__ (buffer.py line 150) — so the two limits can drift and the config can no longer be tuned from Python at all.

Redirect-following loop reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations with no justification, silently breaking deep segment trees

The loop bound was reduced tenfold and the explanatory comment ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:{...}` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop exits with a stale `set_span_id`, and line 40 then writes an incorrect redirect mapping for the incoming span — the span is attached to the wrong segment and the trace is silently assembled incorrectly. There is no error signal when the cap is hit (redirect_depth is returned but nothing distinguishes 'resolved' from 'gave up'). Reducing the guarantee 10x needs at least a metric/alert on `redirect_depth == 1000` or a comment explaining why 1000 is safe; neither is present, and the diff gives no reason for the change.

Direct `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` access will crash the consumer on messages that lack the field

process_batch now reads `end_timestamp_precise` with direct dict indexing. The existing consumer test message did not contain this field until this PR added it, which is evidence that messages without the field are representable in the topic (older producers or schema versions, plus any backlog present at deploy time). A KeyError raised inside process_batch propagates out of the RunTask/multiprocessing strategy and kills the consumer, stalling the whole partition — a much worse failure mode than defaulting the score (e.g. `val.get("end_timestamp_precise") or 0` or falling back to the message timestamp). If the field is guaranteed by the current schema, that guarantee should at least be stated; the current code makes any pre-upgrade buffered message fatal.

The new comment on Cursor.offset states that negative offsets enable "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets". That is not how the module works: _build_next_values and _build_prev_values compute offsets by adding/subtracting the page limit from the current offset, and consumers of these cursors slice querysets where negative offsets are unsupported (raising errors) or silently misbehave. The comment documents a capability that does not exist anywhere in the codebase and will mislead future maintainers into relying on it.

runSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on each target (line 299) before the queries are partitioned by querySupportsSplitting() (line 300). That function excludes queries containing $__range/$__range_ms/$_interval etc. via isQueryWithRangeVariable() precisely so they are NOT time-split (see the comment at lines 285-288: these variables are meant to be resolved by the backend against each sub-request's split time range). applyTemplateVariables runs templateSrv.replace with request.scopedVars, and panel/Explore requests include built-ins like __range in scopedVars, so a query such as count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) is rewritten to a fixed full-range duration (e.g. [2d]) before the guard runs. Concurrent requests from different new devices (or requests hitting different Grafana instances behind a load balancer) can all read a count below the limit and all insert, exceeding the configured device limit by however many requests race in the window. If the limit is meant to be a hard cap (it is now used to deny authentication), the count and insert need to be atomic, e.g. a single conditional upsert or a transaction with a locking read.

With fallbacks enabled, when a key is missing in the current locale the I18n backend walks the fallback chain (user locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en). However I18n.translate in the accelerator only calls load_locale(config.locale), so the fallback locales' translation files stay unloaded unless someone explicitly called I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. That call is only made in ApplicationController#set_locale. Background jobs (Sidekiq), ActionMailer deliveries, rake tasks and console code set I18n.locale directly without ensure_loaded!, so a lookup for a key missing in e.g. :fr will probe :en (or the default locale) while its YAML files are not loaded and will return 'translation missing: fr.xxx' even though the English translation exists. The web UI shows the English fallback while emails/jobs show missing-translation strings. translate should also ensure the fallback locales (I18n.fallbacks[config.locale]) are loaded when fallbacks are configured.

With the new fallback chain, the cached result for a key missing in the user's locale also depends on SiteSetting.default_locale (which is consulted by FallbackLocaleList#[] on every lookup). If an admin changes default_locale at runtime, translations previously resolved through the old default locale remain cached in the process-local LRU cache (size 300, so hot keys persist indefinitely) and users keep seeing the old language until eviction or restart. Nothing invalidates @cache when default_locale changes. The default locale (or a fallback-chain fingerprint) needs to be part of the cache key, or the cache must be flushed when the setting changes.

Any plugin relying on that API will appear to work while its fallbacks are ignored. Either delegate to super for explicitly-set locales or document that per-locale fallback registration is unsupported.

Fallbacks are now enabled in development/test, masking missing-translation regressions, and the PR ships no tests

Previously config.i18n.fallbacks = true was production/profile/cloud66-only; the new initializer enables fallbacks in every environment, including test. As a result, translations missing from a non-English locale now silently render English in the test suite, so tests can no longer detect keys that were not translated or were accidentally removed. On top of that, the PR adds no specs at all for the new behavior: nothing covers FallbackLocaleList ordering (user locale -> default -> en), ensure_loaded!, or that a key missing in the current locale resolves via the fallback chain. Add tests that assert the fallback resolution, and consider asserting on translation-missing detection separately so fallbacks don't hide gaps.

A single SET key 1 EX 60 NX (or a Lua script) should be used instead.

Consequence: for any slot covered by a date override, the host's existing bookings and calendar busy times are never consulted, so a host with a date override who already has a conflicting booking (Cal booking or external calendar event) will still be shown as available and can be double-booked. The override check must not short-circuit the busy check.

The day-match uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD") === slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is explicitly UTC (`.utc()`), but the left-hand side is a plain Dayjs formatted without `.utc()`/`.tz()`, so it renders in whatever timezone the Node process runs in. On a server whose TZ is not UTC (common in non-UTC deployments), the same override/slot pair can land on different formatted days, so the override either fails to match (override ignored, host shown available on an overridden day) or matches the wrong day. Additionally, only the override's *start* day is compared, so an override window that crosses midnight UTC is only applied to one of the two UTC days it spans. The shifted value should be formatted with `.utc()` to match the right-hand side.

`const organizerUtcOffset = dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset();` assumes `override.timeZone` is always set, but this PR adds `timeZone?: string` to `TimeRange` as optional. Any caller of `getSlots` that supplies date overrides without a timezone (which the type explicitly permits — only the `getSchedule` call site populates it) will have dayjs fall back to the process/browser-local timezone for the offset computation, silently producing wrong override windows. In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` is never awaited. `forEach` discards the async callbacks, so the deletion of the organizer's external calendar events and video meetings happens in the background after the mutation has already responded and after the booking row has been marked CANCELLED. The object literal evaluates `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, etc. at module-evaluation time. Dynamic `import()` starts fetching/loading the module as soon as the expression is evaluated, so merely importing `@calcom/app-store` (which videoClient, CalendarManager, the booking handlers, etc. all do) kicks off loading of all 28 app packages immediately — only the binding access is deferred. On the server this means every app dependency is loaded on cold start regardless of which integrations a request uses, and in any client bundle that pulls this module all app chunks are requested at startup. To actually load apps on demand, the store should hold thunks (`applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) that are invoked only for the needed app. Additionally, if one of these eagerly-started imports rejects and that key is never awaited, it surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection.

If `getConnectedCalendars` is not called for a given set of credentials (or is called much later), a rejected import/app-load promise sits unhandled in the meantime, producing unhandled-rejection warnings that can terminate the Node process under default settings. Either await the promise at creation, or attach a no-op catch until it is consumed.

There are no accompanying tests verifying that calendar/video/payment app resolution still works end-to-end (e.g. getCalendar returns a CalendarService for a `google_calendar` credential, getVideoAdapters resolves adapters, payment refund/delete paths resolve the PaymentService). Given that a missed await produces silently broken integrations rather than type errors at runtime call sites like `forEach`, at minimum regression tests for getCalendar, getVideoAdapters, and the booking cancellation/reschedule flows should be added before merging.
